claim: Use only the minimum necessary operational information in every workbook. Do not place unnecessary patient-identifying information, payer portal credentials, or sensitive documents in shared workbooks.
The Control Kits are Excel workbooks. Yellow cells are for your input; teal cells calculate automatically.
When a case in the Pre-Service Clearance Queue needs authorization, record the Queue ID from the Front-End Control Kit on the matching record in the Authorization Tracker.

Your purchase is a one-time purchase of Version 1.1 as described in this document. It does not include future updates or new editions. If a revised edition is released, past buyers may be offered it at a reduced price.
Prior Authorization Control Kit: fixed the 'Open denial/appeal cases' and 'Urgent appeal/deadline cases' counts on the Weekly Authorization Review tab, which did not calculate in the 1.0 build.
Rewrote the Start Here Guide to match the Control Kits tab by tab.

Administrative fee is $15 per party per dispute for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 (previously $115); as of 2026 the IDR entity fee ranges about $200-$840 for single disputes and up to $1,173 for batched disputes.

The en banc Fifth Circuit decided TMA III on August 11, 2026, holding that plans may no longer include non-negotiated 'ghost rates' in QPA calculations, nor categorically exclude retrospective adjustments such as bonuses and incentive payments.

A final rule effective for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 caps batches at 50 line items and allows cross-code-range batching for anesthesiology, radiology, pathology and laboratory services; batched claims must share the same NPI.

According to CMS Federal IDR process status reports, providers prevailed in approximately 80 percent of payment determinations in 2023, approximately 85 percent in 2024 and approximately 88 percent in the first half of 2025.

The Medicare allowable for the CPT code is the most broadly accepted and objectively verifiable benchmark available; start there and frame the IDR offer as a percentage of Medicare, attaching the Medicare fee schedule reference.

Eligible plans are fully insured group, individual market and FEHB plans; self-funded ERISA plans are also covered unless the plan's home state has a qualifying surprise billing law; a UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage claim is a different payer for batching purposes.

The open negotiation notice must be submitted through the CMS IDR portal at federalidrportal.cms.gov within 30 business days of initial payment; negotiation runs 30 business days; IDR must be initiated within four business days after it closes.
Emergency services, non-emergency services at in-network facilities, and air ambulance services are covered under the NSA's IDR process.

As of the 2026 Unified Agenda the Security Rule proposal is not final; HHS moved it to its Long-Term Actions agenda and now targets July 2027 for final action, past the originally anticipated May 2026 date.
The risk analysis must be conducted at implementation of any new billing technology, on significant changes, and, under current OCR guidance and the proposed NPRM, at least annually.
Receive and document the BA's breach notification. Note the date of receipt, this starts the covered entity's own notification clock.
Breaches involving fewer than 500 individuals are reported to HHS annually, by March 1 of the year after discovery; the practice must keep a written log and submit it by that date.
Review each BAA: does it postdate January 25, 2013 (Omnibus Rule effective date)? A BAA that was signed before the 2013 Omnibus Rule does not meet current requirements.
The permissible fee is a cost-based fee covering the labor to copy and the supplies used, not a flat fee or a per-page fee; $1 per page likely exceeds the limit for electronic records.

A covered entity must provide access within 30 days of the request, with a single 30-day extension on written notice; OCR's Right of Access Initiative, launched in 2019, has produced more than 54 enforcement actions.
CMS released an updated Form CMS-R-131 on March 13, 2026, with OMB approval valid through March 31, 2029; it became mandatory May 12, 2026 and use of any prior version is a compliance failure.

A voluntary ABN for a statutorily excluded service is not required, but without one the practice cannot bill the patient if the service is later denied; an unissued voluntary ABN is a guaranteed revenue forfeiture.

When a mandatory ABN is missing or invalid, the result is a billing prohibition that is permanent, non-appealable and complete; there is no administrative remedy, no reconsideration pathway and no recovery mechanism, and the denial is final.
Field C should hold the patient's Medicare Beneficiary Identifier (MBI), or HICN for older beneficiaries not yet transitioned to MBI; the field is optional but completing it is strongly recommended.
Field E consists of reason boxes, one or more of which must be checked (seven quoted reasons are listed); an ABN with an unchecked reason box is invalid.

Blanket ABNs, including a single ABN issued at the start of a course of treatment or calendar year, are not valid under CMS policy; a service-specific ABN must be issued before each service for which denial is anticipated.
When a voluntary ABN is issued for a service later denied, the claim should carry modifier GY to indicate the patient has been notified and may be billed; mandatory ABN situations use GA.

For dually eligible patients an ABN may still be required, and Medicaid rules in most states prohibit billing Medicaid beneficiaries for Medicare medical-necessity denials without a separate, valid financial liability agreement under Medicaid.

CMS may impose civil monetary penalties of up to $10,000 per GFE violation, indexed annually for inflation under 45 CFR part 102; voluntary self-disclosure to CMS has specific procedures and potential penalty mitigation outcomes.
Patients covered by Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE or VA (federal or state government health programs) are exempt from the NSA GFE requirement; separate program protections apply.

Scheduled 10+ business days ahead: GFE within 3 business days of scheduling; 3-9 business days ahead: within 1 business day; request without scheduling: within 3 business days; under 3 business days: no regulatory deadline.

A compliant GFE must contain 10 required content elements, the tenth being an expiration date; there is no federal standard for expiration, and best practice is 90 days for stable services, 30 days for services subject to fee changes.

If the final bill exceeds the GFE by $400 or more, the patient has 120 days from the date of the bill to start a dispute; the $25 administrative fee is paid by the patient; the determination is binding.

Notice of the right to a GFE has three requirements: on the practice website (within two clicks of the homepage), posted in the office, and given at scheduling orally and always in writing; the CMS model notice satisfies them.

Omitting co-provider charges is a compliance failure: a GFE must itemize expected charges of co-providers such as anesthesiologists, pathologists and assistant surgeons who bill separately, listed by name and NPI.

The uninsured and self-pay GFE, notice and dispute requirements have been enforced by CMS since January 1, 2022, while the insured-patient GFE and Advanced EOB requirement is delayed indefinitely, with a proposed rule only targeted as of early 2026.

Once a provider has identified or should have identified an overpayment, it must be reported and returned within 60 days; 'identifies' means when the provider should have known through reasonable diligence; look-back extends up to six years.

A medical director arrangement must meet the AKS personal services safe harbor: written agreement signed by all parties; term of at least one year; compensation set in advance at fair market value; consistent with actual services; not reflecting referral volume.
The Stark non-monetary compensation limit was $519 per physician for calendar year 2025 and $535 for calendar year 2026, covering gifts, meals, entertainment and other non-cash benefits.
False Claims Act civil monetary penalties are up to $28,619 per false claim, the current inflation-adjusted maximum, on top of treble damages.

Before the in-office ancillary services exception can apply, the referring physician must be a member of a group practice with at least two physicians; the ACA patient notice covers MRI, CT, PET, physical therapy and radiation therapy.
Per-click or usage-based equipment rental fees paid to a referring physician can be structured to comply with the Stark rental exception if documented as consistent with fair market value.

Under the Stark recruitment exception, remuneration must be paid directly to the recruited physician (or the physician's new employer), not through a pre-existing practice the physician is joining; any income guarantee must rest on a reasonable income estimate.

CMS's 2020 Stark final rule (effective January 2021) addressed physician compensation plans where productivity exceeds the 75th percentile relative to benchmarks, noting these could receive greater scrutiny.

To diagnose front-end failures, filter denials for CO-4 (service inconsistent with modifier), CO-16 (information missing), CO-22 (coordination of benefits), CO-27 (expenses after coverage terminated) and PR-27 (expenses incurred prior to coverage date).

Clearinghouse rejections: if ANSI error codes 004 (subscriber not eligible), 005 (invalid subscriber ID), or 021 (missing required information) exceed 40% of rejection volume, you have a registration accuracy problem.

Medicare Advantage prior authorization requirements that exceed clinical guidelines and medical necessity criteria that differ from published LCDs are payer design choices; cross-payer denial comparisons support a complaint to the state insurance commissioner.

Contracted payment terms for most commercial payers are 30 days for electronic claims; a payer consistently exceeding them can be escalated, and state insurance commissioners take timely payment violations seriously.

Quarterly write-off audits can recover timely filing write-offs where the payer may accept a late filing with documentation of prior submission attempts; recovery rates on audited write-offs typically run 10 to 20 percent.
Current published data (2024-2025) puts the national average patient collection rate at about 34% to 48%; 45-50% or better is strong, target-level performance and 80% or more is top-quartile.
Cost-to-collect benchmarks for independent practices range from 3% to 8%; a best-in-class range of roughly 2% to 4% is commonly cited by HFMA for the most efficient revenue cycle operations.
Without a formal charge reconciliation process, the gap between encounters and charges is typically 1% to 3% of total encounter volume.
Medicare allows retroactive claims submission for dates of service during the enrollment period under specific conditions.

Even if the practice uses a locum tenens or billing-under-supervision arrangement during the credentialing period... Billing under a supervising physician's NPI is appropriate in some circumstances and inappropriate in others.
Medicare through PECOS, when complete and error-free, typically processes in 30 to 45 days.

practices with documented, standardized prior authorization submission processes achieve first-submission approval rates of 82% to 90%... consistent with the range KFF has reported for 2025 approval rates
Auth Turnaround Time: benchmark < 3 days; > 5 days for urgent cases requires escalation pathway.

When a payer's prior authorization denial rate for a specific service type is materially above the rate for other payers... that is grounds for a formal complaint to your state insurance commissioner.

Calculate the percentage of office visits billed at each level, 99202 through 99205 for new patients, 99211 through 99215 for established patients... The benchmark data is publicly available through CMS and through specialty society publications.
<1% is best-in-class (aspirational)... MGMA/HFMA guidance treats roughly <3-5% of net revenue as the standard benchmark band for most independent practices.

Medicare Advantage plans have the authority to impose prior authorization requirements that exceed traditional Medicare's, to apply medical necessity criteria that differ from published LCDs, and to conduct post-payment audits using criteria not in the original coverage policy.

CMS data analyzed by KFF shows that 80.7% of appealed Medicare Advantage prior-authorization denials were overturned in full or in part in 2024 (above 80% every year 2019-2024), yet only about one in ten denials is ever appealed.
Modifier 25 denials require documentation that the E&M was for a separately identifiable problem not related to the procedure.

An NCCI edit with a modifier indicator of '1' can be separately billed when a modifier appropriately documents distinct services; if the modifier indicator is '0,' the services cannot be unbundled regardless of circumstances.

Payment variance of more than 3% on any code warrants a payer inquiry; a variance consistent over multiple months warrants a formal underpayment dispute and, if unresolved, a state insurance commissioner complaint.
Modifier AS: Assistant surgeon (PA/NP/CRNA); high risk in surgical specialties, credentialing and payer policy dependent.
A physician spending three to five hours per week on authorization-related activities is generating $3,000 to $12,000 per week in lost clinical revenue in most specialty practices.

Medical necessity denials are the most common denial type in specialty billing, and medical necessity, bundling and modifier disputes account for the majority of specialty claim denial volume in most practices.

Collaborative care codes 99492 (first month), 99493 (subsequent months) and 99494 (add-on) pay the psychiatric consulting practitioner for their time; a consultant with a 50-patient caseload can generate $8,000 to $15,000 per month in CoCM billing.
When a psychotherapy add-on (90833, 90836, 90838) is billed with an E/M, the E/M level should be supported by medical decision making or total time, exactly as for any other E/M visit.

Medicare requires HCPCS G0396 and G0397 instead of 99408/99409 for SBIRT; Medicare pays approximately $29 for G0396; the codes are billable in addition to the primary visit code by any provider who performs them.

MHPAEA requires payers to apply prior authorization to behavioral health services no more restrictively than to analogous medical/surgical services; complaints go to the state insurance commissioner (fully insured) or the U.S. Department of Labor EBSA (ERISA self-funded).

A majority of commercial payers now require prior authorization for initial behavioral health evaluations, with concurrent review every 4-8 sessions; TRICARE requires authorization for specialty mental health and typically a PCM referral; traditional Medicare requires none for outpatient psychotherapy.

Audio-only telehealth billed with modifier 95 is an error; the correct modifier is 93 for audio-only where covered; claims need place-of-service code 02 (telehealth) or 10 (telehealth in patient's home).

If more than 60% of individual psychotherapy claims are at 90834 with fewer than 20% at 90837, you likely have a time-documentation gap; the 90834 to 90837 difference is typically $40 to $60 per session.

Group psychotherapy (90853) is reimbursed at approximately 50% to 60% of individual psychotherapy rates; psychological testing codes pay $150 to $300 or more per hour at Medicare rates, $900 to $2,400 for a full evaluation.

TCM codes 99495 and 99496 pay $180 to $280; they require patient contact within two business days of discharge and a face-to-face visit within 14 days (99495) or 7 days (99496); bill them instead of the standard E/M.

Medicare covers advance care planning (99497 first 30 minutes, 99498 each additional 30 minutes) when performed face-to-face by a physician or other qualified health professional; Medicare pays approximately $86 for 99497 and $75 for 99498.
The 90-day billing period codes (93294, 93297, 93298, 93299) are billed once per 90-day period per device; at Medicare rates they pay $75 to $150 per 90-day period depending on device type.

CMS requires a 40-day post-MI and 90-day post-revascularization waiting period for primary prevention ICD implantation; a patient with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, for example, does not have a waiting period.

Nuclear cardiology (78451-78454) requires direct supervision: the physician must be immediately available in the office suite, and a study performed while the supervising physician is at a different office location is not payable; echocardiography requires only general supervision.

The technical component of a nuclear stress test is 55 to 65 percent of total reimbursement; Medicare pays approximately $800 to $1,200 for the technical component of 78452; ICANL accreditation is required by most commercial payers.

For Medicare, the cardiac rehab program must begin within 12 months of the qualifying event; Medicare pays for up to 36 sessions (expandable to 72) at approximately $35 to $50 per session, $63,000 to $90,000 a year for 50 patients.

92921 and 92929 are PCI add-on codes for each additional branch (92929 the most common multi-vessel PCI add-on); 93452 is left heart catheterization with coronary angiography; 93461 is right and left heart cath with coronary angiography and ventriculography.
31231 nasal endoscopy, diagnostic: unilateral or bilateral; modifier 50 if bilateral. 31235 (with sphenoid sinusoscopy) is separately billable with 31231 if both performed.
correct_statement: CPT 31231 is defined as unilateral or bilateral, so modifier 50 is not reported and Medicare pays one fee whether one or both sides are examined (bilateral indicator 2). 31231 is a separate procedure bundled into 31235: the NCCI edit has modifier indicator 0, so the two are never paid together for the same session.
source_title: CMS NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v32.3 (Q4 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.40.7; CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: Little directly (ENT procedure); the same 'no modifier 50, paid once' rule governs 69210 cerumen removal, which geriatrics does bill.

claim: A nasal endoscopy for post-operative debridement falls in the 90-day global period for FESS and is billable only with modifier 58 (staged) or 79 (unrelated).
correct_statement: FESS codes (31254, 31255, 31256, 31267, 31276, 31287, 31288) carry a 0-day Medicare global period, not 90 days. Post-operative endoscopic debridement is CPT 31237 and is separately payable without modifier 58 or 79 after FESS alone. Modifier 79 is needed only when a 90-day procedure such as septoplasty (30520) was performed at the same operation.
source_title: AAO-HNS Position Statement: Debridement (May 13, 2025); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: Little (ENT surgery); the transferable lesson is to read each code's global days in the MPFS instead of assuming 90.

claim: Modifier 50 is billed once at 150 percent of the unilateral fee; two separate lines with RT and LT are each paid at 100 percent of the unilateral fee.
correct_statement: For Medicare, bilateral-indicator-1 procedures are reported on one line with modifier 50 and paid at the lower of the charge or 150% of the fee. Reporting RT and LT on two lines is still paid 150% in total, not 100% each. Codes with indicator 0 or 2 get no bilateral increase. Commercial claim formats vary by payer.
source_title: CMS PFS Relative Value File documentation (RVU26D.pdf, bilateral surgery indicator); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.40.7
practice_impact: Bilateral joint injections (20610-50) and bilateral 69209 pay 150% under Medicare however they are reported; budgeting 200% through RT/LT lines overstates revenue.

claim: 31255 is endoscopic anterior ethmoidectomy with middle turbinate resection, an add-on component; 31267 is endoscopic middle meatal antrostomy; component codes 31254, 31255, 31267, 31276 and 31287 are each billed for the sinus work documented.
correct_statement: 31255 is endoscopic total (anterior and posterior) ethmoidectomy, a stand-alone 0-day code, not an add-on. 31254 is partial (anterior) ethmoidectomy; 31256 is maxillary antrostomy; 31267 is antrostomy with tissue removal. On the same side, 31255 with 31276 or 31287 must be reported as 31253 or 31257/31259, and 31254 is bundled into 31255.
source_title: AAO-HNS CPT for ENT: Changes to the FESS and BSD Family of Codes for CY 2018; CMS NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v32.3; CMS NCCI Policy Manual 2026 Ch. 5
practice_impact: Little (ENT surgery).

claim: 69631 is tympanoplasty without mastoidectomy with ossicular chain reconstruction; 69641 tympanoplasty with mastoidectomy with ossicular chain reconstruction; 69660 stapedectomy with footplate drill-out; 42415 total parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation; 92602 cochlear implant programming age 7 and over.
correct_statement: All five are wrong. 69631 and 69641 are WITHOUT ossicular chain reconstruction (69632/69633 and 69642 include it). 69660 is stapedectomy without drill-out; 69661 is with footplate drill-out. 42415 is lateral-lobe parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation; 42420 is total. 92602 is reprogramming for patients under 7; 92603/92604 are for age 7 and older.
source_title: AAO-HNS Clinical Indicators (Mastoidectomy, Tympanoplasty, Stapedectomy, Parotidectomy); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D; CMS Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners data
practice_impact: Little (ENT surgery and audiology codes).

claim: Inspire hypoglossal nerve stimulator: FDA indications and payer criteria align closely - AHI between 15 and 65, BMI below 32 (some payers up to 35), CPAP failure, no complete concentric collapse at the palate on drug-induced sleep endoscopy.
correct_statement: On June 8, 2023 FDA expanded the Inspire indication to AHI 15-100 and raised the recommended BMI limit from 32 to 40. Medicare LCDs, including First Coast L38398 for Florida, still require AHI 15-65, BMI under 35, age 22 or older, CPAP failure or intolerance, and no complete concentric collapse on DISE. FDA and payer criteria no longer align.
source_title: FDA Recently-Approved Devices: Inspire Upper Airway Stimulation - P130008/S090; First Coast LCD L38398 Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for the Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
practice_impact: Little for billing; when referring Medicare patients with sleep apnea in Florida, coverage stops at BMI under 35 and AHI 65 despite the broader FDA label.

claim: 31231 pays a Medicare rate of $115 per procedure; in-office balloon sinuplasty pays Medicare rates of $400 to $600 per sinus; 31579 pays $100 to $200 more than 31575 at Medicare rates.
correct_statement: 2026 Medicare national rates: 31231 pays $193.39 in the office and $54.78 in a facility (Florida office $189-$208). Office balloon dilation 31295/31296/31297 pays about $1,565-$1,603 per code (Florida $1,506-$1,686) before multiple-endoscopy reductions; facility $124-$152. 31579 pays $67.80 more than 31575 in the office ($195.06 versus $127.26).
source_title: CMS Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File RVU26D (October 2026 release) and CY 2026 GPCI file
practice_impact: Little (ENT codes), but it shows the vendor's dollar figures have no traceable fee-schedule origin; recompute any revenue estimate from the current MPFS.

claim: 69210 is removal of impacted cerumen requiring instrumentation, one ear, and simple irrigation is not billable; 69209 is removal of cerumen using irrigation, one ear, at lower reimbursement.
correct_statement: Both codes require impacted cerumen: 69210 is removal requiring instrumentation, unilateral; 69209 is removal by irrigation/lavage, unilateral, so irrigation of impacted wax is billable (2026: $17.03 versus $47.76 office). Removing non-impacted wax is not separately billable. Medicare pays 69210 once whether one or both ears (bilateral indicator 2); 69209 takes modifier 50.
source_title: CMS NCCI Policy Manual for Medicare Services 2026, Chapter 11; CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: Direct: cerumen removal is routine in facility geriatrics. Bill 69210 once per session regardless of ears, document impaction, and expect about $48-$52 at office or nursing-facility POS 32 and $28-$31 at SNF POS 31 in Florida.

claim: 99483: 'Billable separately from E&M on same day.' Combining 99483, advance care planning (99497) and a 99215 visit in a single appointment can generate approximately $540 to $580 in Medicare revenue; 'This is not upcoding.'
correct_statement: 99483 cannot be billed on the same day as office/outpatient E/M (99202-99215), home visits (99341-99350) or advance care planning (99497/99498); the NCCI edits carry modifier indicator 0, so no modifier bypasses them. The appointment pays 99483 alone: $292.93 national non-facility in 2026 ($290.61 Rest of Florida; about $170-$185 facility). Billing all three is unbundling.
source_title: CMS, Cognitive Assessment & Care Plan Services (page last modified 10/07/2026); NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v323r0 (effective Oct. 1, 2026); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D and 2026 GPCIs (released 08/26/2026); NCCI Policy Manual for Medicare Services 2026, Ch. I
practice_impact: Following the guide overstates revenue by about $280 per combined visit: 99215 and 99497 deny under NCCI, and splitting or re-dating them to get paid would be false-claims exposure; in a facility place of service 99483 pays only about $173-$185 in Florida, and its use for nursing-facility residents should be confirmed with First Coast.

claim: An Advance Beneficiary Notice (ABN) 'must be issued to the patient before the service is provided' whenever 'a service may not be covered by Medicare or an MA plan'.
correct_statement: The ABN (Form CMS-R-131; current version expires 03/31/2029) is for Original Medicare only. CMS bars its use by MA plans or contracted providers; for MA enrollees the provider or patient must request a plan organization determination. In Original Medicare it is mandatory only for specific expected denials (medical necessity, frequency limits, custodial care), optional for statutorily excluded services.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 30 §§50.1-50.2.1; CMS FFS ABN page (last modified 07/17/2026) and Form CMS-R-131 (Exp. 03/31/2029); CMS Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance §40.12.1 (effective July 6, 2026)
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage patients an ABN does not shift liability: absent a plan denial notice or a clear Evidence of Coverage exclusion the enrollee owes a contracted provider nothing, so staff trained on this page would collect money that must be refunded or written off.

claim: Denial pattern: CCM (99490/99491) billed in the same month as TCM (99495/99496) for one patient; because TCM includes care management, 'the two cannot be billed in the same calendar month'.
correct_statement: Since January 1, 2020 Medicare allows CCM (99487, 99489, 99490, 99491, 99439) to be billed for the same patient during the 30-day TCM period (99495/99496) when medically necessary, provided the same time is not counted twice. The prohibition applied only through 2019; the NCCI edits were deleted effective 12/31/2019. CCM still cannot overlap with care plan oversight G0181/G0182.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet, Chronic Care Management Services (MLN909188, June 2025); CY 2020 PFS final rule, 84 FR 62568, 62685-62687 (Nov. 15, 2019); CMS Transitional Care Management Services page (last modified 10/29/2026); CMS CCM FAQ (8/16/2022); NCCI PTP Edits v323r0
practice_impact: Suppressing CCM in every TCM month forfeits about $66 per patient-month for 99490 (about $44 in a facility setting) on the post-discharge patients who most need care management; verify each MA plan's own edits before assuming it follows Medicare.

claim: Medicare is always primary. Medicaid is the payer of last resort. Never bill the patient for the balance on a dual-eligible claim; Medicaid's payment (often $0) is the final settlement.
correct_statement: Medicare pays before Medicaid, but not always first: employer group plans, workers' compensation, no-fault and liability insurers can be primary under Medicare Secondary Payer rules. Federal law bars billing QMBs for Medicare cost-sharing even when Medicaid pays $0, but SLMB-only, QI and QDWI patients still owe coinsurance and deductibles. States may charge QMBs nominal copays. Verify QMB status each visit.
source_title: CMS, Provider Enrollment and Third Party Liability FAQs for Dually Eligible Individuals (version 01/14/2025); CMS MLN006977, Beneficiaries Dually Eligible for Medicare & Medicaid (June 2024); CMS QMB Program page (last modified 03/16/2026); CMS Medicare Secondary Payer overview; 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii); MLN Connects (Oct. 22, 2026); Fla. Stat. §§409.908(13), 409.907(3)(j) (2026)
practice_impact: Facility panels are heavily dual: billing a QMB invites sanctions, but blanket write-offs forgo collectible coinsurance from SLMB-only/QI patients, and CMS warned on 10/22/2026 that people who lose Medicaid or QMB status lose the protection, so eligibility and other primary coverage must be checked at each date of service.

claim: A geriatric practice with heavy Medicare Advantage volume operates in a multi-payer commercial environment where every plan has its own rules and none of them are required to follow Medicare's.
correct_statement: MA plans set their own networks, prior authorization lists and contracted rates, but 42 CFR 422.101 requires them to cover all Part A and B services and comply with NCDs, applicable LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules; internal criteria are allowed only where Medicare's are not fully established. Non-contract providers must accept Original Medicare amounts as payment in full.
practice_impact: Treating MA plans as unbound by Medicare rules means not appealing medical-necessity denials of 99483, CCM, TCM or skilled nursing care that meet Medicare criteria; 42 CFR 422.101 is the practice's strongest appeal citation, while payment terms still come from each contract.

claim: CCM requires written patient consent, obtained and documented before CCM services begin; this consent must be renewed if the patient changes providers.
correct_statement: Written consent has not been required since January 1, 2017. CMS accepts verbal or written consent, documented in the medical record with the required disclosures (availability of CCM, cost-sharing, one billing practitioner per month, right to stop). Consent is obtained once, before CCM starts, and again only if the patient switches to a different billing practitioner.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet, Chronic Care Management Services (MLN909188, June 2025); CMS FAQ on Practitioner Billing for Chronic Care Management Services (last updated 8/16/2022); CY 2017 PFS final rule, 81 FR 80170, 80250
practice_impact: Requiring a signed form is stricter than Medicare and stalls CCM enrollment of facility residents who cannot easily sign; documented verbal consent is enough, and CMS confirms CCM is billable for patients in skilled nursing, nursing facility and assisted-living settings.

claim: Core CPT Code Reference lists as current Medicare-paid codes: G0505 cognitive assessment ($232-$250), 99358 prolonged non-face-to-face service ($110-$118), and 99339/99340 'Care plan oversight - home health/hospice' ($55-$104).
correct_statement: None of the three is payable by Medicare in 2026. G0505 existed only for 2017 and was replaced by 99483 on January 1, 2018 (same service). 99358 has had status I, not valid for Medicare, since 2023. 99339/99340 were domiciliary/home supervision codes, always bundled, deleted in 2023. Medicare's home health and hospice oversight codes are G0181/G0182, about $110.
source_title: CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D (October 2026 release) and RVU22A/RVU23A; CY 2018 PFS final rule, 82 FR 52976, 53077 (Nov. 15, 2017); CY 2023 PFS final rule, 87 FR 69404, 69440 and 69610 (Nov. 18, 2022)
practice_impact: Charge masters or projections built on these rows produce rejected or zero-paid claims; bill care plan oversight with G0181/G0182 and non-face-to-face work through care management codes (CMS's TCM page still mentions 99358/99359, but the fee schedule marks them not payable).

claim: TCM requires medication reconciliation within two business days of discharge, documented as a completed activity, not an intention.
correct_statement: Only the interactive contact with the patient or caregiver has a two-business-day deadline. Medication reconciliation and management must be furnished on or before the date of the face-to-face visit, which falls within 7 calendar days (99496) or 14 calendar days (99495) of discharge. It must be documented as performed.
source_title: CMS, Transitional Care Management Services (web page that replaced MLN908628; last modified 10/29/2026); First Coast Service Options, Checklist: Transitional care management (TCM) (April 30, 2026)
practice_impact: A 2-day reconciliation rule makes staff drop valid TCM claims (99495 pays about $220 and 99496 about $299 nationally, non-facility, in 2026) when reconciliation was done at the visit; TCM applies only after discharge to a community setting (home, rest home, assisted living), not to a patient still in a skilled nursing facility.

claim: High-complexity MDM (99215) requires multiple chronic conditions with exacerbation risk or one condition with severe exacerbation risk; prescription drug management with risk of adverse effects; and independent interpretation of tests or independent historians. Virtually every active neurology patient qualifies.
correct_statement: The listed criteria describe moderate MDM (99214): chronic illness with exacerbation or two stable chronic illnesses, prescription drug management, one data category. High MDM (99215) needs two of three: severe exacerbation or threat to life or bodily function; extensive data (two of three categories); high risk such as drug therapy requiring intensive toxicity monitoring.
source_title: AMA CPT Evaluation and Management (E/M) Code and Guideline Changes (2023), Levels of MDM table; CMS CY2025 Evaluation and Management Codes by Specialty
practice_impact: High: the same MDM table governs 99215 and nursing-facility 99310; the vendor's test would bill moderate visits as high. Nationally geriatric medicine bills 99215 on 22% of office visits and 99310 on 12% of nursing-facility visits.

claim: CCM is billable for any patient with two or more chronic conditions; it requires 20 or more minutes of clinical staff time per calendar month; CCM pays approximately $62 per month per patient (99490).
correct_statement: 99490 needs at least 20 minutes of clinical staff time per calendar month, but also two or more chronic conditions expected to last 12 months that pose significant risk, documented consent, an initiating visit, a comprehensive care plan, certified EHR and 24/7 access. Only one practitioner may bill per month. 2026 payment is $66.13 non-facility, $43.76 facility.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet: Chronic Care Management Services (MLN909188, June 2025); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: High: CCM is core geriatrics revenue. Florida pays about $66-$71 a month at office, home, ALF or nursing-facility POS and $45-$48 for SNF Part A (POS 31); another practice may already hold the single monthly billing slot.

claim: TCM: 99495 (moderate complexity, face-to-face within 14 days) or 99496 (high complexity, face-to-face within 7 days), both requiring documented patient contact within two business days of discharge; TCM pays $80 to $150 more than a standard follow-up visit.
correct_statement: Confirmed. 99495 needs at least moderate MDM and a face-to-face visit within 14 calendar days; 99496 needs high MDM and a visit within 7 days; both need interactive contact within 2 business days. 2026 non-facility rates are $220.11 and $298.60, about $85-$106 above 99214/99215. Only one practitioner may bill, and discharge must be to a community setting.
source_title: CMS Transitional Care Management Services (web page, last modified 10/29/2026); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: Usable with limits: CMS lists home, domiciliary, rest home and assisted living as the community settings, with SNF and nursing facility only as discharge-from settings, so TCM mainly fits home and ALF patients; one biller per discharge.

claim: 95812 is EEG awake and drowsy up to 40 minutes (standard routine EEG); 95813 over 40 minutes; 95816 awake and asleep up to 40 minutes; 95819 awake and asleep over 40 minutes; 95827 all-night recording; 95830 ambulatory EEG.
correct_statement: 95812 is extended EEG, 41-60 minutes; 95813 is extended EEG, 61-119 minutes; 95816 is routine EEG awake and drowsy; 95819 is routine EEG awake and asleep; 95827 was deleted effective January 1, 2020; 95830 is insertion of sphenoidal electrodes. Ambulatory and long-term EEG have been reported with 95700-95726 since 2020.
source_title: CMS Medicare Coverage Database: Billing and Coding: Special Electroencephalography (A56771); First Coast Billing and Coding: Special EEG Tests (A57667); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D
practice_impact: Little for geriatrics billing; it matters only when ordering EEGs, and it shows the vendor's code tables cannot be used without checking.

claim: Drug codes: ocrelizumab J3030; ofatumumab J3031; methylprednisolone IV J1020-J1030; eculizumab J1300; lecanemab billed with unclassified J3490 or J3590, REMS enrollment required; amyloid PET scan A9588.
correct_statement: Ocrelizumab is J2350; J3030 is sumatriptan and J3031 is fremanezumab. Ofatumumab IV is J9302. IV methylprednisolone is J2919; J1020-J1040 were the acetate form and ended 3/31/2024 (now J1010). Eculizumab is J1299 since 4/1/2025. Lecanemab is J0174, with no REMS but a CMS registry requirement. A9588 is fluciclovine; amyloid tracers are A9586, Q9982, Q9983.
source_title: CMS HCPCS Quarterly Update: October 2026 Alpha-Numeric HCPCS File; FDA Approved REMS list (REMS@FDA); CMS NCD 200.3
practice_impact: Moderate: joint injections with methylprednisolone acetate must be billed as J1010 per 1 mg (J1020/J1030/J1040 ended 3/31/2024), and dementia patients on lecanemab need J0174 plus CMS registry submission.

claim: For BOTOX (J0585), total billed units must equal the sum of documented per-site units; any difference between note and claim generates a denial or recoupment.
correct_statement: The administered-units line must match the per-site units in the note, and First Coast requires each injection site with its dosage. But BOTOX comes in single-dose vials: Medicare requires discarded units on a separate line with modifier JW and documented waste, or modifier JZ when nothing is discarded, so total billed units can properly exceed injected units.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, Billing and Coding: Botulinum Toxins (A57715, effective 11/09/2025); CMS JW/JZ Modifier Policy FAQ; CMS October 2026 Part B Payment Limit File
practice_impact: Applies to every single-dose Part B drug the practice buys and bills: JW or JZ is mandatory. For a 155-unit migraine dose from a 200-unit vial, the 45 discarded units are worth about $293.

claim: Needle EMG is billed by extremity count with 95860-95864 alongside nerve conduction codes 95907-95913; 95885 and 95886 are 'combined' codes for EMG with NCS, and 95885 is rarely preferred.
correct_statement: 95860-95864 are for needle EMG when no nerve conduction study is done that day. When NCS (95907-95913) is performed, EMG is reported with add-on codes 95885 (limited), 95886 (complete, five or more muscles) or 95887 (non-extremity). NCCI edits bar 95860-95864 with 95907-95913 with no modifier override. Nothing supports calling 95885 rarely preferred.
source_title: CMS NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v32.3 (Q4 2026); First Coast Billing and Coding: Nerve Conduction Studies and Electromyography (A57123)
practice_impact: Little for geriatrics billing; useful only when reviewing electrodiagnostic referrals or outside claims.

claim: If the payer upholds an MS drug denial after peer-to-peer, file a complaint with the state insurance commissioner and notify the patient of the right to an independent external review.
correct_statement: External review covers non-grandfathered commercial plans only after the internal appeal is exhausted (peer-to-peer is not an appeal), requested within four months. In Florida it runs through the HHS-administered federal process or accredited IROs, and the state regulator cannot act on Medicare Advantage, Medicaid or self-funded plans. Medicare Advantage denials go to plan reconsideration, then CMS's independent review entity.
source_title: 45 CFR 147.136; CMS CCIIO State External Appeals Review Processes; Florida DFS Division of Consumer Services; 42 CFR 422.592
practice_impact: High: most geriatric patients are in Medicare or Medicare Advantage, where a state insurance complaint has no effect; use plan reconsideration, the independent review entity and Part D exception requests.

claim: Visits beyond that count ... are separately billable using CPT 59425 (4-6 additional antepartum visits) or 59426 (7 or more additional antepartum visits).
58572: Laparoscopic hysterectomy, uterus 250g or less, with BSO - BSO included; do not bill 58661 separately.
Medicare ... covers ... annual well-woman exams under the Medicare preventive benefit ... gynecologic preventive services (pap smear G0101, pelvic exam Q0091).
Medicare does not cover obstetric services for its beneficiaries (Medicare patients are, by definition, over 65 and not pregnant).
Included in Global OB Package: Postpartum office visit (one, within 6 weeks) ... Routine newborn care (professional, if same physician).

A standard obstetric ultrasound (76805) has a total Medicare payment of approximately $120 - split roughly equally between professional and technical components ... billing the technical component ... requires AIUM ... accreditation or equivalent, which most commercial payers require.
N80.0 (endometriosis of uterus) and N80.1 (endometriosis of ovary) are different authorization submissions even in the same patient.
The correct billing: 99395-99397 (preventive, age-appropriate) with modifier 25 on the additional E&M code (99212-99215) for the separately identified problem.

Complex Chronic Care Management (CCM) - 99487 and 99489 - is billable for patients with two or more chronic conditions ... when the practice provides at least 20 minutes of clinical staff care management time per month.

complex CCM (99487) pays approximately $132-144 for the first 60 minutes, and $70-79 for each additional 30 minutes (99489) ... 99490 pays approximately $62/month, with add-on code 99439 at approximately $47

G0023 (first 60 minutes of navigation per month), G0024 (each additional 30 minutes) ... The revenue is $80 to $130 per patient per month ... For a practice with 150 active patients ... $144,000 to $234,000

covered by Medicare under codes 99497 (first 30 minutes) and 99498 (each additional 30 minutes) ... the note must state that an ACP conversation occurred, describe the nature of the discussion, and document the time spent.

high-complexity MDM: multiple chronic conditions with exacerbation risk, prescription drug management with adverse effect monitoring, and independent interpretation of test results. That is a 99215 by MDM criteria, regardless of visit length.
Trastuzumab IV (J9355) and trastuzumab subcutaneous (Q5117) are different codes. Table: Bevacizumab (Avastin) J9035, billed per mg; Doxorubicin, liposomal, J9001.
Medicare and most commercial payers allow billing for the discarded portion of single-use vials when the waste is documented in the medical record and the claim includes a JW modifier

the patient must have a non-myeloid malignancy, must be receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy, and the hemoglobin must be below 10 g/dL at the time of initiation ... myeloid malignancy (AML, MDS, CML) ... outside Medicare coverage criteria

An ultrasound-guided injection 'revenue stack' is the injection code (20610, 20611, 27096 or other) plus ultrasound guidance code 76942 plus a separately identifiable E&M; the guidance code is the component most often missed.
correct_statement: 76942 cannot be stacked on these codes. An ultrasound-guided major-joint injection is 20611 alone (guidance included); 20610 is the no-ultrasound code; 27096 already includes fluoroscopic or CT guidance. NCCI bundles 76942 into 20610, 20611 and 27096. An E/M is payable only with modifier 25 for significant, separately identifiable work beyond the decision to inject. 'Most often missed' is unsourced.
source_title: CMS NCCI Policy Manual for Medicare Services 2026, Ch. IV (H.7, I.29) and Ch. I Section D; NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v32.3 (Q4 2026); CMS RVU26D
practice_impact: Relevant if the practice gives joint injections: with ultrasound bill 20611 alone (about $104 non-facility or $50 facility nationally, 2026); adding 76942 to 20610/20611 is an NCCI unbundling error, and a same-day E/M needs modifier 25 with separate work.

claim: Surgeons frequently perform multiple separately reportable arthroscopic procedures in one session, e.g. 'a meniscectomy and a chondroplasty'; modifier 59 or XS may override an NCCI edit for anatomically distinct sites within the same joint.
correct_statement: Chondroplasty is not separately reportable with meniscectomy: CPT 29880/29881 include chondroplasty in any compartment, and NCCI bars 29877 with other knee arthroscopy codes (edit modifier indicator 0, no bypass). Modifier 59/XS works only for limited knee pairs in different compartments; edits between two arthroscopy codes on the same shoulder may not be bypassed, with three exceptions.
source_title: CMS NCCI Policy Manual for Medicare Services 2026, Chapter IV Section E (Arthroscopy); NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v32.3 (Q4 2026)
practice_impact: Little (no arthroscopy in a geriatrics practice), but it shows the vendor's bundling examples cannot be relied on without checking NCCI.

claim: Under modifier 51, standard multiple procedure payment rules are 'typically 100% for the highest-value procedure, 50% for the second procedure, 25% for the third and subsequent procedures.'
correct_statement: Medicare's multiple-surgery rule is 100% for the highest-valued procedure and 50% for the second through fifth; the 25% tier was the pre-1995 rule. Endoscopy/arthroscopy families follow a separate base-code rule. UnitedHealthcare's standard is also 100/50/50. The 100/50/25 formula is Florida Medicaid's rule and an alternate method used by some plans.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 12 section 40.6; Florida AHCA 2026 Practitioner Fee Schedule; UnitedHealthcare MPPR policy 2026R0034D
practice_impact: Check same-day multiple-procedure payments by payer: Medicare should pay 100/50/50, Florida Medicaid 100/50/25; contract terms govern Medicare Advantage and commercial plans.

claim: Spine add-on codes for additional levels (22614, 22632, 22634) and for 'bone graft procurement (20931, 20936, 20937, 20938)' are separately reportable, full-value codes not subject to multiple procedure reduction.
correct_statement: 22614, 22632 and 22634 are add-on codes paid without multiple-procedure reduction. But Medicare bundles 20936 (local autograft) and 20930: status B, no payment. Only 20931, 20937 and 20938 pay separately (about $98 to $163 nationally in 2026), one unit each per operative session. 20931 is structural allograft, not graft procurement.
source_title: CMS 2026 National Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File, October release (RVU26D); NCCI Policy Manual 2026 Ch. IV Section H
practice_impact: little

claim: For implants billed by practice-owned facilities, pass-through and markup rules vary by payer: 'Medicare has specific rules limiting implant markup.'
correct_statement: Medicare has no markup allowance. In ASCs, implants are packaged into the procedure payment and separately billed implants are denied; only devices with OPPS pass-through status are paid separately, contractor-priced at acquisition cost or invoice (no markup). In offices, supplies are built into practice-expense RVUs. Markup percentages are a commercial-contract concept.
source_title: 42 CFR 416.164 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 14, Ambulatory Surgical Centers
practice_impact: little

claim: 97000-series physical medicine codes (therapeutic exercise, therapeutic activities, manual therapy, neuromuscular reeducation) 'are billable when performed by or incident to a physician' if documentation supports necessity and time and payer policy permits.
correct_statement: Physicians may bill 97000-series codes, but Medicare covers therapy incident to a physician only when the person treating meets therapist qualifications (graduate of a PT/OT/SLP program). Athletic trainers, medical assistants and PTAs/OTAs billed incident-to do not qualify. Plan-of-care rules, the $2,480 KX threshold (2026) and the 50% practice-expense reduction also apply.
source_title: Medicare Benefit Policy Manual (Pub. 100-02) Ch. 15 section 230.5; CMS Therapy Services page (CY 2026 KX threshold and MPPR); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 6
practice_impact: Do not bill Part B therapy codes for SNF residents: PT/OT/SLP must be billed by the SNF even when furnished or supervised by a physician; elsewhere only therapist-qualified staff count for incident-to therapy.

claim: A complex new spine evaluation with outside-record review, detailed exam and imaging/conservative/surgical plan 'supports a 99205'; coding it 99203 or 99204 forfeits $80 to $120 per encounter, or $200,000 to $300,000 a year at ten new patients daily.
correct_statement: Under current CPT/CMS rules the level is set only by medical decision making or total time; exam detail does not count. 99205 needs high MDM or 60-74 minutes; planning elective major surgery without identified risk factors is moderate risk (99204). 2026 Medicare gap to 99205: $59 from 99204, $119 from 99203. Only 4% of orthopedic new-patient visits are billed 99205.
source_title: CMS MLN006764 Evaluation and Management Services (May 2026); CMS RVU26D; CMS CY 2025 E&M Codes by Specialty; AMA CPT E/M guidelines (MDM table)
practice_impact: The same MDM-or-time rule governs nursing-facility codes 99304-99310; blanket up-coding advice is audit exposure. CY2025 geriatric-medicine benchmark: 99309 is 54.5% and 99310 is 12.4% of subsequent NF visits.

claim: Medicare Advantage plans add prior authorization for orthopedic procedures 'that traditional Medicare does not require authorization for' and apply 'medical necessity criteria that differ from Medicare's published LCDs.'
correct_statement: MA plans may require prior authorization that traditional Medicare mostly lacks (exceptions: the hospital-outpatient list including cervical fusion and facet joint interventions; the WISeR model in six non-Florida states since 1/1/2026). But plans must follow NCDs and LCDs; since coverage year 2024 internal criteria are allowed only where Medicare criteria are not fully established and must be public.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101 and 422.138 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); 88 FR 22120 (Apr 12, 2023); CMS WISeR Model page; CMS hospital OPD prior authorization page
practice_impact: High for an MA-heavy Florida panel: appeal MA denials that apply criteria stricter than the First Coast LCD or an NCD, citing 42 CFR 422.101(b)-(c), and ask for the plan's published internal criteria.

claim: DTaP has three components: bill '90460 x1 + 90461 x2 (or 90471 x1 + 90472 x2)'; Standard 2 says 90461 and 90472 add-on units 'are counted per component, not per injection.'
correct_statement: 90460/90461 are counted per vaccine component, so DTaP is 90460 x1 plus 90461 x2. But 90471/90472 are counted per vaccine (single or combination), so DTaP alone is 90471 x1; 90472 is never per component. Under CMS's 2012 rule VFC administration is a flat fee per vaccine; Medicaid payment of 90461 varies by state.
source_title: AAP, Frequently Asked Questions for the Pediatric Immunization Administration Codes (Sept 2025); CMS final rule 77 FR 66670 (Nov 6, 2012)
practice_impact: Little: 90460/90461 apply only through age 18. Adult vaccines are billed per vaccine (90471/90472); Medicare Part B flu, pneumococcal, hepatitis B and COVID shots use G0008-G0010 and 90480.

claim: A problem raised at a well-child visit (ear, rash, behavioral concern) is billable as 99212-99215 with modifier 25 alongside the preventive code; standard: bill the modifier 25 E&M 'on every encounter where a problem was addressed.'
correct_statement: CPT allows 99202-99215 with modifier 25 alongside a preventive code only when the problem is significant enough to require additional, separately documented work; insignificant or trivial problems are not separately reportable. A blanket 'every encounter' standard overstates the rule. Medicare does not cover 99381-99397 at all.
source_title: AAP, Coding for Pediatric Preventive Care (2020, quoting CPT preventive medicine guidelines); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 section 30.6.2; NCCI Policy Manual 2026 Ch. I and XI
practice_impact: Medicare does not pay 99381-99397; when a problem visit is billed with a covered preventive service, the same significant-and-separately-identifiable modifier 25 test applies, so bill it case by case, not on every encounter.

claim: Billing the vaccine product code (e.g., 90700) for a VFC-supplied vaccine 'is a compliance violation'; the practice 'may bill only the administration fee for VFC vaccines.' VFC covers Medicaid-eligible, uninsured and underinsured children.
correct_statement: VFC providers may not charge for the cost of VFC vaccine and may charge only an administration fee (Florida federal cap $24.01). Reporting the product code is not itself a violation: Florida Medicaid requires both product and administration codes and pays the product at $0.00. Eligibility also includes American Indian/Alaska Native children; underinsured children qualify only at FQHCs/RHCs.
source_title: Florida AHCA Prescribed Drugs Immunization Fee Schedule (effective July 1, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 1396s; CMS final rule 77 FR 66670
practice_impact: little

claim: 98008-98015 audio-only E&M codes are billable for calls with established patients involving medical decision-making, not if a visit follows within 24 hours; most commercial payers cover them; they replaced 99441-99443 deleted January 1, 2025; after-hours calls average $35 (98008-98010).
correct_statement: 99441-99443 were deleted 1/1/2025. But 98008-98011 are audio-only codes for new patients and 98012-98015 for established patients; all require more than 10 minutes of medical discussion. The 7-day/24-hour restriction belongs to 98016, not these codes. Medicare (status I) and UnitedHealthcare do not pay 98000-98015; Cigna does. The $35 average is unsourced.
source_title: CMS CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 89 FR 97710 (Dec 9, 2024); CMS RVU26D; UnitedHealthcare Replacement Codes Policy 2026R0128A; Cigna R31 Virtual Care
practice_impact: Medicare rejects 98000-98015: bill audio-only visits as office E/M with modifier 93 (home audio-only allowed through 12/31/2027), or 98016 for 5-10 minute check-ins (about $17 nationally in 2026).

claim: 'After-hours modifier 33 or add-on code 99050-99060' can be billed as an after-hours supplement for services outside normal business hours where the practice has established after-hours availability.
correct_statement: Modifier 33 is the preventive-services modifier (it waives cost-sharing), not an after-hours modifier. 99050 (after posted hours), 99051 (scheduled evening/weekend/holiday hours) and 99053 are adjunct special-service codes, not CPT add-on codes; 99056-99060 are not after-hours codes. Medicare bundles all of them (status B, no payment); Florida Medicaid pays 99050 and 99051 $8.27.
source_title: CMS 2026 Relative Value File (RVU26D); CMS MLN909289 Advance Care Planning (March 2026); Florida AHCA 2026 Practitioner Fee Schedule
practice_impact: Medicare pays nothing extra for after-hours codes (status B), so there is no after-hours supplement on Medicare facility visits; never append modifier 33 to non-preventive services.

claim: CCM eligibility is 'two or more chronic conditions expected to last at least 12 months'; it requires at least 20 minutes of clinical staff time per calendar month, a care plan and patient/guardian consent; school forms and specialist coordination count.
correct_statement: CCM requires two or more chronic conditions expected to last 12 months or until death that also place the patient at significant risk of death, acute exacerbation/decompensation or functional decline, plus 20 minutes of clinical staff time monthly (99490), a comprehensive care plan, documented consent, an initiating visit and 24/7 access. Only care-management activities count; school-form completion is unverified.
source_title: CMS MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services (June 2025); CMS FAQs on Practitioner Billing for CCM (Aug 16, 2022); CMS RVU26D
practice_impact: Directly usable: CMS says CCM may be billed for nursing-facility and assisted-living residents; 99490 pays $66.13 non-facility or $43.76 facility nationally in 2026 if consent, care plan and initiating visit are documented.

claim: If an audit finds 90460 billed where the physician did not personally counsel, 'the recoupment applies to every encounter in the audit period - not just the sample.'
correct_statement: Recoupment beyond sampled claims happens only through statistically valid sampling and extrapolation, and is an estimate, not every encounter. Medicare may extrapolate only after finding a sustained or high error level or failed education; Florida Medicaid law permits sampling and extension to the population; commercial audits depend on contract. 90460 counseling may be by a physician or other qualified professional.
source_title: Medicare Program Integrity Manual (Pub. 100-08) Ch. 8 section 8.4; Florida Statutes section 409.913(20) (2026); 42 CFR 401.305
practice_impact: Extrapolation is a real but conditional and appealable risk in Medicare and Florida Medicaid audits of any systematic documentation gap; separately, identified Medicare overpayments must be returned within 60 days (6-year lookback).

claim: G0444 is listed as 'Annual depression screening, 15 min', Medicare-covered; 99421-99423 online digital E&M are described as 5-10, 11-20 and 21-30 minutes cumulative over 7 days, requiring patient-initiated contact.
correct_statement: G0444's current descriptor is 'Annual depression screening, 5 to 15 minutes'; Medicare covers it once per 12 months in primary care settings with no cost-sharing. 99421-99423 are for established patients, patient-initiated, cumulative over 7 days: 5-10, 11-20, and 21 or more minutes (not 21-30).
source_title: CMS October 2026 Alpha-Numeric HCPCS File; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 18 section 190; NCD 210.9; CY 2020 PFS final rule 84 FR 62568
practice_impact: G0444 is payable only in office-type or telehealth places of service (02, 10, 11, 19, 22, 49, 71), so it denies on nursing-facility or assisted-living visits; it pays about $18.70 non-facility in 2026.

claim: A TCM claim cannot be submitted until after the face-to-face visit, but must be submitted with the date of discharge as the service date.
correct_statement: CMS requires the TCM claim (99495/99496) to carry the date of the required face-to-face visit, not the discharge date. The claim may be submitted once that visit is furnished and need not be held to day 30. The 30-day service period starts on the day of discharge; interactive contact is due within two business days.
source_title: CMS, Frequently Asked Questions about Billing the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule for Transitional Care Management Services (March 17, 2016); CY 2016 PFS final rule, 80 FR 70921; CMS MLN Transitional Care Management Services page (modified 10/29/2026)
practice_impact: Dating TCM to the discharge day mis-reports every claim and invites denials or overlap with discharge-day and facility billing; TCM also applies only when the patient returns to a community setting (home, assisted living), not on hospital-to-SNF or nursing facility transfers.

claim: A physician managing a patient on prescription drug management, which includes virtually every chronic disease patient on any medication, is performing moderate MDM by definition; an established chronic illness is at minimum moderate MDM, supporting 99214.
correct_statement: Prescription drug management is only an example of moderate risk, one of three MDM elements; two of three must be met. One stable chronic illness is low complexity. Moderate MDM (99214, or 99309 in nursing facilities) also needs moderate problems or data, for example two or more stable chronic illnesses or one with exacerbation, and a documented drug decision.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, Medical Decision Making and the Impact of Prescription Drug Management (September 23, 2026); AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes, Table 1 Levels of Medical Decision Making (effective January 1, 2023)
practice_impact: Following this would upcode stable, single-problem refill visits (true level 99308 or 99213) to 99309 or 99214 across the panel: overpayment refunds, First Coast medical review and False Claims Act exposure. The same MDM table governs nursing facility and home visit codes.

claim: The first 30 minutes of ACP conversation in a calendar year bills at 99497. Additional 30-minute increments bill at 99498. The revenue is $50 to $80 per encounter under Medicare.
correct_statement: 99497 is the first 30 minutes of each ACP encounter (16-45 minutes) and 99498 each additional 30 (from 46 minutes). There is no calendar-year rule and no frequency limit; only the cost-sharing waiver is tied to the annual wellness visit. 2026 allowed amounts: $86.84 non-facility, $65.80 facility nationally; Florida $86.87-$92.82 and $66.75-$70.92.
source_title: CMS MLN909289 Advance Care Planning fact sheet (March 2026); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D and CY 2026 Florida carrier file (MAC 09102); CMS ACP billing FAQ (July 14, 2016); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71186-71190
practice_impact: ACP is billable in nursing homes and assisted living and can be repeated when health status or wishes change, so a once-a-year habit forfeits revenue; at SNF place of service 31 expect about $67-$71 in Florida. From January 1, 2027 clinical-staff ACP time moves to G0572/G0573.

claim: Incident-to billing pays 100% of the physician fee schedule versus 85% under the NPP's own NPI, and requires that the physician is physically present in the office suite during the NPP's service and established the plan of care.
correct_statement: The payment split is right: incident-to pays 100%, NP/PA direct billing 85%, and the physician must initiate the course of treatment and stay involved. But since January 1, 2026 direct supervision may be virtual, through real-time audio/video (not audio-only), except for 010/090-day global services. Incident-to is unavailable for hospital or SNF patients.
source_title: 42 CFR 410.26 and 410.32(b)(3)(ii) (eCFR current to November 6, 2026); CMS CY 2026 PFS final rule fact sheet (CMS-1832-F); First Coast, Incident-to service guidelines (March 9, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12 sec. 30.6.13.E; 42 CFR 414.52 and 414.56
practice_impact: Largely unusable in facility work: incident-to E/M visits in SNF or nursing facility settings are not payable, so NP/PA facility visits bill under their own NPI at 85%. Billing them at 100% under the physician is an overpayment and False Claims Act risk.

claim: CCM requires documented monthly contact totaling at least 20 minutes, a current comprehensive care plan, patient consent on file, and billing that submits the service in the calendar month it was performed.
correct_statement: 99490 requires at least 20 minutes of clinical staff care-management time per calendar month (not patient contact), two or more qualifying chronic conditions, a comprehensive care plan, consent documented once, an initiating visit for new or unseen-in-a-year patients, certified EHR and 24/7 access. Claims are billed once per month and need not be submitted within the service month.
source_title: CMS, Frequently Asked Questions About Practitioner Billing for Chronic Care Management Services (last updated August 16, 2022; still posted on CMS's care management page, modified November 3, 2026); CMS MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services booklet (June 2025)
practice_impact: CMS allows CCM for SNF, nursing facility and assisted living residents, billed at the place of service where the practitioner ordinarily sees them; counted minutes must come from the practice's own or contracted clinical staff, and the vendor's checklist omits the initiating visit and 24/7 access.

claim: AWV required components: health risk assessment, review of medical and family history, list of current providers and medications, measurement of cognitive function, detection of depression risk factors, and a written personalized prevention plan.
correct_statement: Listed items are real but incomplete. The first AWV (G0438) also requires height, weight, BMI and blood pressure, a functional ability and safety review, a written 5-10-year screening schedule, a risk-factor list, personalized advice and referrals, review of current opioid prescriptions, substance-use screening, and ACP if the patient wishes. Cognition is assessed by observation; no test is mandated.
source_title: 42 CFR 410.15 (eCFR current to November 6, 2026; last amended 90 FR 50007, November 5, 2025); CMS Annual Wellness Visit provider page (modified April 9, 2026)
practice_impact: AWVs can be furnished to facility residents (G0439 about $137-$147 in Florida in 2026), but a template built on the vendor's six items would fail review for missing measurements, functional and safety, opioid and substance-use elements.

claim: The national benchmark for primary care is approximately 30% of established patient visits at 99213 and 45% at 99214, per the CMS Medicare Physician and Other Supplier Public Use File; 60% or more at 99213 signals systematic undercoding.
correct_statement: CMS's CY 2025 Part B E/M-by-specialty data put family practice at 28.5% 99213 and 63.9% 99214; internal medicine 26.8% and 62.7%; geriatric medicine 16.9%, 57.7% and 22.1% at 99215. The vendor's 45% understates 99214 by about 18 points. A 60% 99213 share is an outlier, but only documentation proves undercoding.
source_title: CMS, CY 2025 Evaluation & Management (E&M) Codes by Specialty, Medicare Part B Physician/Supplier National Data (CY 2025 claims; page modified August 28, 2026); CY 2024 and CY 2019 editions for trend
practice_impact: Office codes are the wrong yardstick for facility work. CMS 2025 subsequent nursing facility visits, geriatric medicine: 99307 6.3%, 99308 26.9%, 99309 54.5%, 99310 12.4%; nurse practitioners 3.0%, 32.7%, 56.1%, 8.1%. Benchmark against those, with documentation, not against 99214.

claim: A practice with 300 CCM-eligible Medicare patients, billing 99490 at the current Medicare rate, generates approximately $150,000 to $230,000 per year in additional revenue.
correct_statement: The 2026 national 99490 rate is $66.13 non-facility and $43.76 facility (Florida $65.97-$70.95 and $44.58-$47.66). Billing all 300 patients every month gives at most about $238,000 allowed, $157,500 at the facility rate, including 20% coinsurance and before staff cost. The vendor's range assumes 63-97% monthly capture; real-world uptake is far lower.
source_title: CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D (October 2026) and CY 2026 carrier file for Florida (MAC 09102); ASPE/NORC, Analysis of 2019 Medicare FFS Claims for CCM and TCM Services (March 2022); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71174-71175
practice_impact: For 300 residents at SNF place of service 31 the Florida ceiling is about $160,000-$172,000 a year, not $230,000; at the 30.7% reach of practices that actually bill CCM it is roughly $50,000-$78,000 gross, before care-manager payroll and uncollected coinsurance.

claim: Every laboratory claim for Medicare and Medicare Advantage patients is checked against the relevant LCD; no claim with a non-covered diagnosis goes out without an ABN on file or a clinically supported covered-diagnosis substitution.

Independent practices that purchase interpretations from a radiologist or laboratory and bill the purchased service to Medicare at a marked-up rate violate the anti-markup rule; the practice may only bill at its actual purchase cost.
HbA1c (83036) billed for a patient without a diabetes diagnosis: the covered indications are established diabetes monitoring, not pre-diabetes screening, at most MACs.

Lipid panel (80061) billed with 'family history of hyperlipidemia' (Z82.49) rather than the patient's own hyperlipidemia diagnosis (E78.5): family history alone does not establish coverage for a lipid panel at most MACs.
CMS paused the AUC program's claims-based enforcement effective January 1, 2024, and later rescinded the AUC regulations; AUC non-compliance 'currently carries no direct claim denial risk'.

ACR accreditation, or equivalent accreditation from the Intersocietal Accreditation Commission, is required by most commercial payers and many Medicare Advantage plans as a condition for billing the technical component of advanced imaging.

The technical component of an outpatient MRI represents 50 to 60 percent of total Medicare reimbursement; 50 MRI studies per week at a Medicare technical component rate of $350 per study yields $910,000 a year.

A Level V (88307) pathology code requires that the specimen type appear in the 88307 specimen list (colon segment, kidney, lung lobe, thyroid gland, and others); the worked example is a colon resection for adenocarcinoma.

The ultrasound report 'is the document that supports the 76942 billing code' for a guided knee injection; the guidance code (20604, 20606, 20611, or 76942) is billed on every encounter where documentation is complete.

The difference between 20610 (major joint injection, no imaging) and 20611 (with ultrasound guidance) is $60 to $100 per procedure at Medicare rates; 30 guided injections a week at $80 yields $124,800 a year.
Rituximab (J9312): billed per 100mg. Belimumab IV, Benlysta (J0490): billed per mg.
Methylprednisolone IV (J1020-J1040): dose-dependent J-code; document dose and indication.

Rheumatology infusion visits are billable E&M encounters in addition to the drug and administration codes; the assessment supports 99213 or 99214 at minimum for virtually every infusion patient, and 80 percent is a conservative estimate.
The CCM revenue for a practice with 200 enrolled patients, billing at the standard 99490 rate of $62 per month: $12,400 per month, $148,800 per year.

Every patient with RA, SLE, PsA, or AS has at minimum two chronic conditions when the cardiovascular comorbidity burden is considered, and that burden is universal; the panel qualifies overwhelmingly for CCM.

MDM elements that rheumatology visits routinely generate include independent interpretation of laboratory results (CBC, metabolic panel, anti-dsDNA, complement levels, drug levels); the majority of established visits support 99214 or 99215.

CARC 16 (claim lacks information) or CARC 252 (referring/ordering provider not found): missing NPI, missing authorization number, or incomplete claim data. This is a claim completion problem, usually a practice management system configuration issue.

CARC 96 (non-covered charge) or CARC 167 (this diagnosis is not covered) is a front-end coverage verification failure or a diagnosis code problem; CARC 96, 167 and 272 are grouped as 'coverage and eligibility' front-end denial patterns.
CARC 50 (non-covered services because this is not deemed a 'medical necessity' by the payer) is a documentation or medical-necessity-criteria problem, not a prior-authorization problem.

CARC 197 (precertification/authorization/notification absent): the claim was submitted without an authorization that this payer requires; either a workflow failure or a policy change making authorization newly required.
CARC 18 (duplicate claim) or CARC 97 (payment included in another service): your billing team is submitting the same claim twice, or the payer considers a billed service bundled into another.
CARC 29 (the time limit for filing has expired): the claim was submitted after the payer's timely filing deadline. This is a charge entry lag problem.
In a typical practice with eight to twelve contracted payers, the top two denial-generating payers account for 60 to 70 percent of total denial volume.
Ten re-worked denials per biller per day is sustainable. Fifty is not.
Clean claim rate measures the percentage of claims that pass through your clearinghouse and are accepted by the payer on the first submission: no rejections, no missing information, no edit failures.
A rejection happens before adjudication: the clearinghouse or payer finds a technical or structural problem and returns the claim without processing it. A denial happens after adjudication.
Authorization failures generate a specific and highly visible rejection class that is entirely preventable when the authorization workflow is functioning correctly.
Invalid diagnosis code: the ICD-10 code is missing a required digit, is an invalid code for the date of service, or is a header code that cannot be used on a claim.
Every rendering provider, billing provider, and referring provider in the system should have an NPI that matches the CMS NPPES database and the enrollment records at each contracted payer.
Re-submitting a rejected claim with the same error generates a second rejection and, at some payers, triggers a duplicate claim flag that complicates the eventual correct submission.
If your practice management system is reporting a clean claim rate above 95% but your denial rate is above 8%, those two numbers are in conflict.
Clean claim rate predicts the other metrics 30 to 60 days in advance. A clean claim rate that drops in January will show up as elevated Days in AR in February and elevated denial rate in March.
Medicare typically pays within 14 days of a clean claim.
Some Medicare Advantage plans take 30 to 45 days [to pay a clean claim].
Some Medicaid programs take 60 or more [days]; these are structural delays that cannot be fixed by the practice.
Aged AR that is not resolved within 90 to 120 days of service typically becomes uncollectable (filing window closed, appeal deadline passed, or account sent to collections).
Any denial past the appeal window is not workable - it should be written off and documented as a process failure.
Every claim that fails on first submission adds 20 to 45 days to its AR age.
Raising clean claim rate from 87 to 94 percent 'will see days in AR drop by 5 to 8 days within 60 days without any other intervention'.
A contract paying 5 percent above market rate on a 45-day cycle 'may generate less actual cash per quarter' than one paying market rate on a 21-day cycle.
For most commercial payers, the appeal deadline is 90 to 180 days from service date.
Clean claims submitted to most payers will pay or deny within 14 to 30 days.
Payers with 365-day timely filing windows have claims that are genuinely recoverable at 150 or 180 days.
For 0-30 day claims, verification that the claim was received and is in process 'can be batch-checked via ERA rather than individually worked'.
Historical recovery rate for the 120-plus day bucket is 'typically 30 to 50 percent for most independent practices'.
Most practices use $100 minimum for collections referral.
When an account is referred to collections or written off, 'the documented contact history is the compliance record that demonstrates due diligence'.
A new provider whose claims concentrate in the 61-plus day buckets within their first 60 days has a credentialing gap (NPI not active with a payer, wrong taxonomy codes, or fee schedule not loaded).

Research across independent practices consistently shows the probability of collecting a patient balance in full drops from about 95% at time of service to 70-80% after a first statement, 50-60% after a second, and 30-40% in collections.
A copay collection rate below 95% means the front desk is not collecting money the practice has an absolute right to collect at every visit.
A POS collection rate above 90% is best practice, is achievable, and should be the target for every independent practice.
A $200 balance sent through two statements and a collections referral yields $60 to $80 gross; after a typical 25 to 40 percent agency fee the net recovery is $36 to $60.
Every patient with a known balance (copay, prior balance, or estimated deductible) is told the amount and asked for payment before they are roomed.
For balances above $200 the front desk immediately offers a payment plan, such as $50 per month, with automated monthly charges to the card on file.

Collectible means the patient is not on a payment plan, financial assistance program, or hardship waiver that legitimately defers collection; a written charity care policy with income thresholds lets the practice keep a firm standard.

Without active management, most practices' POS collection rate settles between 60 and 70 percent, and a team trained to 90 percent can fall to 65 percent within 60 days of one experienced staff departure.
In many independent practices, patient responsibility now represents 20 to 35 percent of total revenue.
Research consistently shows statements received within 30 days of service produce payment rates 25 to 35 percentage points higher than those received after 60 days.
Every dollar that passes through the statement cycle costs $8 to $15 to collect and recovers at a fraction of face value.
The collections agency recovers 20 to 35 cents on the dollar on average; recovery rates below 20 percent should prompt consideration of a different agency.
Every account that meets the referral criteria (minimum balance, days from service, completed statement series, no active payment plan) is referred to collections without exception.
A patient collection rate above 90% is best practice and is still achievable in a high-deductible environment; below 60% is structural failure.

A written payment plan policy sets minimum payment, maximum duration and whether interest is charged; most practices charge no interest for plans under 12 months, with automatic monthly charges to a card on file.
ERA enrollment is free and is the single most impactful administrative change most practices have not completed.
For write-offs coded 'denial appeal expired' or 'timely filing', the quarterly recovery review asks: 'Is there a balance transfer to patient responsibility that was never executed?'
Rejected claims, claims returned before adjudication, restart their AR clock when resubmitted, but the original service date governs the timely filing deadline.
Every denial that is categorized as appealable must have an appeal filed within 30 days of receipt ... A filed appeal stops the clock on the appeal deadline.
Accounts written off as 'denial appeal expired' may have a secondary recovery path, including 'a small claims or arbitration option for large amounts'.
Any timely filing write-off is a 100% preventable revenue loss, the claim was never denied for clinical or coverage reasons.
