Bad debt (uncollected patient): below 3% of net revenue is acceptable; 3% to 5% is a warning zone; above 5% of net revenue is the action threshold.

Timely filing write-offs above 0.5% of gross charges and expired-appeal denial write-offs above 1% of gross charges are action thresholds; preventable write-offs should be less than 5 percent of total write-offs.
The recovery rate from these retrospective reviews is typically 10 to 15 percent of the dollar amount reviewed.
Net Collection Rate = (Payments Received) / (Charges Billed minus Contractual Adjustments).
A 5 percent improvement in clean claim rate typically produces a 1 to 2 percent improvement in net collection rate with a 60-day lag.

Patient responsibility is commonly estimated at roughly 20 to 35 percent of net collectible revenue for most practices ... A patient collection rate of 75 percent means ... a direct 5 to 9 percent drag on net collection rate.
A practice with a net collection rate of 97 percent ... commands a higher valuation multiple than a peer practice at 89 percent with the same clinical volume.

A primary care practice with 45 percent Medicaid volume will have a structurally lower achievable net collection rate ... because Medicaid's lower rates and higher administrative burden create a different collection environment.
The percentage of AR over 120 days is the most predictive leading indicator of net collection rate. [Unworked aged AR] will become write-offs within one to two quarters.
The decomposition in Section 2 will almost always reveal one component that contributes 40 to 60 percent of the total collection gap.
Every payer has a timely filing deadline - typically 90 days, 180 days, or one year from service date, depending on the payer.
some Medicare Advantage plans require submission within 90 days, some commercial payers within 60 days

For any service within 30 days of its timely filing deadline: enter the charge immediately and submit the claim the same day, regardless of documentation completeness; most payers allow medical record submissions to support pending claims.
A claim that misses the timely filing deadline because someone was waiting for a complete note is not recoverable at any documentation quality level.
Same day or next day (0-1 days) is best practice; 1-2 days acceptable; 3-5 days is the action threshold; above 5 days is a significant problem.
A practice with a 4-day average charge lag has every claim starting its AR clock 4 days late. The practice reports 42 days in AR. The effective AR age - from service date to payment - is 46 days.
hospital progress notes completed within 24 hours of the encounter, operative notes completed and dictated within 24 hours of the procedure, discharge summaries completed within 24 hours of discharge

The monthly surgical charge reconciliation shows a discrepancy rate below 2 percent... A reconciliation discrepancy rate above 5 percent means the intraoperative charge capture workflow is not functioning consistently.
Collections agency commissions: variable by contract terms, typically around 1 percent of collections referred.
Industry benchmarks for claims per FTE per month range from 750 to 1,200 for outpatient practices depending on complexity.

A rejected claim that must be corrected and resubmitted costs approximately three to five times as much in billing staff time as a clean claim... A denied claim that requires an appeal costs five to ten times as much.

Staff cost (salaries + benefits + management overhead): typically 70 to 80 percent of total billing cost in in-house operations... Technology cost (PMS, clearinghouse, eligibility tools, patient portal): typically 10 to 15 percent.

Establish a small balance write-off threshold... balances below the threshold [$25 or $50] receive one automated statement and are written off if not paid within 30 days, without any manual follow-up.
In a well-managed billing operation, rework activities should consume no more than 25 to 30 percent of total billing staff time.

Cost to collect should include all direct and allocated costs of the revenue cycle function: billing staff salaries and benefits, management overhead, clearinghouse fees, statement costs, practice management system fees, collections agency commissions, and outsourced billing fees.
Many practices that outsource billing do so at a higher cost to collect than their internal operation
Our coders and providers are current on the 2021 E&M guideline changes and correctly apply the medical decision-making pathway.
Copays are collected at check-in, before the patient is roomed, at every visit, with no exceptions.
Patient responsibility now represents 25 to 35 percent of revenue in most independent practices, and that percentage is growing as high-deductible plans continue to dominate the market.
Total score 31, 46 (AT RISK): 'Likely costing $50,000, $150,000 annually in preventable revenue loss.' Total score 47, 61 (MODERATE): 'Likely $20K, $50K recoverable annually.'
Our overall patient collection rate is at or above 90% of patient responsibility billed.
We offer structured payment plans with automatic payment required, not open-ended 'send us what you can' arrangements.
Our patient payment portal allows a patient to click a link, see their balance, and complete payment in under two minutes, without requiring a username, password, or portal login.
Our charge lag standard is defined in writing (target: ≤48 hours for office encounters, ≤5 business days for hospital and procedure encounters) and monitored by provider.
Industry benchmarks from MGMA and HFMA: median days in AR 45, 55 vs top quartile 30, 38; median clean claim rate 85, 90% vs >96%; median initial denial rate 8, 12% vs <5%.

For a practice billing $4 million annually, the difference between median and top-quartile performance on these three metrics 'can represent $200,000 to $400,000 in additional annual collections'; called 'the documented revenue gap.'

Benchmark targets by practice size: small (<3 providers) days in AR 35, 45, clean claim 90, 93%, denial 7, 10%, net collection 94, 96%, AR over 90 days <20%; large (10+) days in AR 40, 52, net collection 96, 98%.
Clean claim rate: the percentage of claims submitted that are accepted by the payer on first pass without rejection, denial, or request for additional information.
Each payer has timely filing limits, and denials based on timely filing are almost never overturned.
CARC (Claim Adjustment Reason Code) and RARC (Remittance Advice Remark Code) on every denial explanation of benefits 'tell you exactly why the claim was denied.'
For 1, 2 providers: 1, 2 billing staff covering all functions, or outsourced. Full outsourcing is often more cost-effective at this size.
A denial that must be appealed costs 25, 45 minutes of staff time and delays payment 30, 60 days; every dollar invested in denial prevention typically returns 3, 5x in avoided denial management cost.
Medicare's deadline is one year from the date of service. Most commercial payers range from 90 to 180 days, and some managed care contracts impose 60-day windows.
Payers may deny for late filing and, 'absent a documented administrative error exception, those denials are final'; 'A timely filing denial is not an appeals opportunity. It is a forfeiture.'
Review denials for timely filing reason codes - CO-29 on Medicare remits, or equivalent commercial denial codes.
HFMA-aligned industry estimate: 1 to 5 percent of collectible revenue is lost to charge capture failure. On $2 million in collections, that is $20,000 to $100,000 per year.
A gastroenterologist performs a colonoscopy with polyp removal - the primary procedure is billed, the polypectomy add-on is missed.

Office 'injectable medications, diagnostic supplies, or procedure kits' are 'items that have specific HCPCS codes and separate reimbursement'; unbilled supplies and implants are costs 'your payer contracts allow you to recover'.

'For a statistically meaningful sample, pull 25 to 30 encounters per provider being audited', chosen from highest-revenue service types, then 'extrapolate to annual volume to estimate the full-year revenue impact'.
The charge master 'should be reviewed at minimum annually' to confirm 'All CPT and HCPCS codes are current - codes are added, deleted, and revised annually'.
E&M MDM Score Key: 0, 2 pts = Level 2 | 3, 4 pts = Level 3 | 5, 7 pts = Level 4 | 8, 9 pts = Level 5.

Rubric criteria: Risk 'Low (prescription drug management, minor surgery with identified risk)'; Data 'Extensive (independent interpretation of results OR discussion of management with external provider)'; Problems 'High (... new problem with uncertain prognosis ...)'.
Listed as an undercoding pattern: 'Failing to capture the complexity of prescription drug management, particularly controlled substances, as a high-risk MDM element.'
'New patient codes require higher MDM thresholds but are consistently coded at lower levels out of unfamiliarity.'

'OIG's own published guidance for physician practices suggests a 5, 10 record minimum per payer'; a sample of 25-30 records is said to give 'a stronger statistical base' for a comprehensive internal audit.
False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733) imposes civil liability of up to three times the amount of the false claim plus penalties per claim; 'knowingly' includes reckless disregard.
OIG's Self-Disclosure Protocol 'provides a mechanism for practices to voluntarily report and repay overpayments, typically at a reduced multiplier' compared with a government-initiated investigation.

Medicare requires submission within one year of the date of service; Medicare Part B redetermination: 120 days from date of denial; reconsideration (Level 2): 180 days from date of redetermination decision; QIC reconsideration 'takes 60 days to resolve.'
correct_statement: Part B claims must be filed within 1 calendar year after the date of service. Redetermination: 120 calendar days from receipt of the initial determination notice (receipt presumed 5 days after the notice date). Reconsideration: 180 calendar days from receipt of the redetermination notice. The QIC decides within 60 calendar days, extended up to 14 days per later evidence submission.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 424.44, 405.942, 405.962, 405.970 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'New provider roadmap: Appeals' (Oct. 20, 2025)
practice_impact: Safe to calendar as written (the vendor's wording is about 5 days conservative); but ignore the playbook's nearby line that the one-year limit still runs during an appeal, and note Medicare untimely-filing denials are not appealable (Claims Processing Manual ch. 1, sec. 70.4).

claim: A Medicare Advantage plan 'is required by 42 CFR 422.101 to provide coverage at least as generous as traditional Medicare for all Part A and Part B services'; denying such a claim 'violates that requirement.'
correct_statement: 42 CFR 422.101(a)-(c) requires MA plans to cover all Part A and B services except hospice and kidney acquisition costs, follow NCDs, LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules, and not deny on other criteria. Plans may still require prior authorization, use networks, and apply public internal criteria where Medicare's are not fully established; a denial is not automatically a violation.
practice_impact: A real lever for MA medical-necessity denials if the appeal cites 422.101(b)-(c) plus the specific NCD/LCD; it does not defeat prior-authorization, network or contract denials, and the practice's Part B claims for MA enrollees who have elected hospice go to Original Medicare (First Coast), not the plan.

claim: Medicare Advantage denials: the escalation pathway runs through the MA plan's internal appeal process first, then to an Independent Review Entity designated by CMS, [then] the same multi-level Medicare appeal system that applies to traditional Medicare.
correct_statement: For enrollees and non-contract providers (who must waive enrollee liability), the path is plan reconsideration (request within 60 days), automatic IRE review (C2C since May 1, 2026), then ALJ ($200 threshold in 2026), Appeals Council and federal court ($1,960). A contracted provider's payment denial with no enrollee liability is outside this process; the provider contract's dispute terms govern.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 422.562, 422.582, 422.592, 422.600-422.612 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, 'Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance' (effective July 6, 2026); 90 FR 55869 (2026 amount-in-controversy thresholds)
practice_impact: High: for in-network MA claims the IRE/ALJ ladder is not available to the practice; use each plan's contractual dispute process and deadlines, and reserve the Subpart M route for pre-service requests on the patient's behalf or out-of-network claims with a waiver of liability.

claim: QIC reversal rates for well-supported clinical denials are materially higher than MAC redetermination reversal rates.
correct_statement: CMS data show the opposite in aggregate. For Part B in 2025, 45% of decided MAC redeterminations were fully favorable (3% partially) versus 24% of QIC reconsiderations (1% partially); in 2024 it was 43% versus 20%. Only DME shows a higher QIC rate. CMS publishes no rates for 'well-supported clinical denials,' so that qualifier cannot be tested.
source_title: CMS, 'Original Medicare Claim Appeals Data - 2025' and '- 2024' (Appeals Fact Sheets ZIP on the 'Second Level of Appeal: Reconsideration by a QIC' page, modified Sept. 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not expect better odds at the QIC for physician claims; put the full record into the redetermination, and file everything by reconsideration because evidence first offered after the QIC level can be excluded.

claim: The ACA established the right to independent external review for most commercial insurance denials that have exhausted the internal appeal process... IRO decisions are binding on the payer in most states.
correct_statement: The ACA (PHS Act 2719) gives enrollees in non-grandfathered plans external review, but only for denials involving medical judgment, rescissions, or No Surprises Act compliance, not most denials. The IRO decision binds the plan under every compliant state process and under the federal process. Florida has no qualifying state process; its issuers use the HHS-administered or accredited-IRO federal process.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 147.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-19; CMS/CCIIO external appeals page with state-by-state process list
practice_impact: Little: external review does not reach Medicare, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid; for the few commercial patients it is the patient's request (practice as authorized representative), due within four months, through the federal process rather than a Florida state program.

claim: [MHPAEA] requires that commercial health plans apply the same coverage standards, prior authorization requirements, treatment limitations, and reimbursement rates to [behavioral health] services as they apply to comparable medical and surgical services.
correct_statement: MHPAEA bars financial requirements and treatment limits on mental health/substance use benefits that are more restrictive than the predominant ones applied to substantially all medical/surgical benefits in a classification; prior authorization and rate-setting processes must be comparable and no more stringently applied. It does not require equal reimbursement rates or any behavioral coverage, and does not apply to Medicare.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 146.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 78 FR 68240 (Nov. 13, 2013) preamble; CMS MHPAEA page (modified Mar. 13, 2026); Departments' statement of non-enforcement of the 2024 rule's new provisions (May 15, 2025)
practice_impact: Little: parity is a commercial-plan (and Medicaid managed care) tool and does not apply to Medicare, the practice's dominant payer; where it does apply, argue that the limitation is not comparable, never that rates must be equal.

claim: A claim that is denied, appealed, and reversed costs an average of $25 to $118 in staff time to manage ... and is collected 30 to 90 days later
correct_statement: The endpoints are two unrelated, dated estimates: about $25 to rework a claim (MGMA figure cited since at least 2015; $25.20 in a 2021 MGMA article) and $118 per appealed claim (Change Healthcare, 2016 hospital data). Premier's hospital surveys report $43.84 (2022) and $57.23 (2023) per denied claim. No source supports a 30-to-90-day delay.
source_title: MGMA, '4 keys to driving down denials' (Dec. 19, 2018) and MGMA Stat (Mar. 18, 2021); AAFP FPM 2015;22(2):7-10; Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb. 2025)
practice_impact: Fine as a rough argument that prevention beats rework, but do not put $25-$118 or 30-90 days into ROI math; time the practice's own appeals and track days from denial to payment by payer.

claim: Typical % of total denials: Administrative / front-end errors 37, 38%; Medical necessity 22, 23%; Coding and billing errors 17, 18%; Coverage / non-covered service 11, 12%; Coordination of benefits 6, 8%; Timely filing exceeded 4, 5%.
correct_statement: No published source gives this distribution. The closest benchmark, Change Healthcare's 2022 index of hospital claims, shows registration/eligibility 22%, missing or invalid claim data 16%, documentation requests 14%, authorization 13%, service not covered 11%, medical necessity 6%, coding 5%, untimely filing 4%. KFF's 2024 marketplace data put medical necessity at 5% of in-network denials.
source_title: Optum, 'Actionable Insights & Strategies From the Change Healthcare 2022 Denial Index' (HFMA Texas, May 2023); KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); Massachusetts Health Policy Commission DataPoints on 2024 claim denials
practice_impact: Do not benchmark against this table: its medical-necessity share (22-23%) is about four times published figures and none of the data are physician- or Medicare-specific; build the practice's own mix from remittance CARC/RARC codes by payer.

claim: CY2026 conversion factors are $33.57 (qualifying APM) and $33.40 (non-qualifying APM).
correct_statement: Correct for CY2026: $33.5675 (qualifying APM participants) and $33.4009 (all other clinicians), in force through Dec. 31, 2026. CMS's CY2027 final rule (published Nov. 9, 2026) lowers them to $32.95 and $32.63 on Jan. 1, 2027 (-1.83% and -2.31%) because the one-year 2.5% increase expires.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F), Oct. 31, 2025; CY2027 figures from CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F), Nov. 2026
practice_impact: Benchmark at $33.40 unless clinicians are Qualifying APM Participants; on Jan. 1, 2027 the non-QP factor drops to $32.63, so the fee schedule and every Medicare benchmark must be rebuilt for 2027.

claim: The increase reflects a temporary 2.5% payment bump enacted by Congress through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a small MACRA statutory update, and a positive budget-neutrality adjustment.
correct_statement: Correct. The CY2026 factors combine MACRA updates of +0.75% (qualifying APM) or +0.25% (others), a one-year +2.5% increase under Public Law 119-21 sec. 71202 (popularly the One Big Beautiful Bill Act; CMS says Working Families Tax Cut legislation) and a +0.49% budget-neutrality adjustment. The 2.5% covers 2026 services only; no enacted extension found as of Nov. 10, 2026.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F); Public Law 119-21, sec. 71202 (govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm); CY 2026 PFS final rule, 90 FR 49960-49961
practice_impact: The 2.5% bump ends Dec. 31, 2026; unless Congress acts, 2027 Medicare payment per RVU falls about 2.3% for non-QP clinicians, which belongs in the 2027 budget.

claim: For Original Medicare, the correct position is to bill above the Medicare allowed amount at the chosen multiplier... if the billed charge is below the Medicare allowed amount, the payment is limited to the billed charge.
correct_statement: Medicare bases payment on the lesser of the actual charge or the fee schedule amount, so a charge below the allowance forfeits money. Participating providers may bill any higher charge. But nonparticipating providers on unassigned claims may not charge above the limiting charge, 115% of the nonpar amount (109.25% of par), so a 200-250% multiplier is unlawful there.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.21 and 414.48 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Fee schedule par, nonpar, and limiting charge explanation' and 2026 Florida locality 99 fee schedule; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20
practice_impact: A participating practice loses nothing by charging above the fee schedule; any nonparticipating clinician must cap unassigned Medicare charges at the limiting charge or risk civil penalties up to $19,940 per knowing violation (latest HHS inflation adjustment, 45 CFR 102.3) and exclusion.

claim: The Medicare fee schedule has separate rates for facility settings (hospital outpatient, ASC) and non-facility settings (physician office). The non-facility rate is higher because it includes the practice expense component covering office overhead.
correct_statement: Some PFS codes have separate facility and non-facility rates, set by place-of-service code. Both include practice expense; facility PE RVUs are smaller because the facility bears most direct costs and, since 2026, CMS halves work-based indirect PE. Facility includes hospitals, ASCs and SNF Part A stays (POS 31); nursing facility (POS 32), assisted living and home are non-facility.
source_title: CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule, 91 FR 70992 at 71018-71020 (Nov. 9, 2026), citing Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20.4.2 (cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c12.pdf); 42 CFR 414.22(b)(5); CMS 2026 relative value file RVU26D
practice_impact: Nursing-home visits split by POS: in 2026 CPT 99309 is allowed $114.90 in POS 32 but $99.58 in POS 31 (Rest of Florida locality); CMS equalizes 99304-99310 and 99315-99316 on Jan. 1, 2027, so benchmark charges to the higher non-facility rate.

claim: Payment = (Work RVU + Practice Expense RVU + Malpractice RVU) × Geographic Practice Cost Index × Conversion Factor
correct_statement: There is no single GPCI. Payment = [(Work RVU x Work GPCI) + (PE RVU x PE GPCI) + (MP RVU x MP GPCI)] x CF. Each component has its own locality index; 2026 Florida GPCIs (work/PE/MP) are Miami 1.000/1.041/2.529, Fort Lauderdale 1.000/1.013/1.808, Rest of Florida 1.000/0.956/1.503.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 12, sec. 20.1 Method for Computing Fee Schedule Amount; 42 CFR 414.26(d); CMS CY 2026 GPCI file (Addendum E, RVU26D release)
practice_impact: Florida's malpractice GPCI (1.50-2.53) dwarfs its work and PE indices, so use First Coast's locality fee schedule, not a one-index shortcut; the 1.0 work GPCI floor lapses Jan. 1, 2027 (Rest of Florida 0.977) unless Congress extends it.

claim: Increasing billed charges does not violate payer contracts, practices are generally free to set and adjust their own charges.
correct_statement: Practices generally set their own charges; fee-schedule contracts usually pay the lesser of billed charge or contracted rate, so a uniform increase normally breaches nothing. That is contract-specific (some cap increases or require notice), and law limits charges: Medicare's nonparticipating limiting charge, OIG exclusion authority for Medicare/Medicaid charges substantially above usual charges, and Florida PIP's reasonable-charge rule.
source_title: 42 CFR 1001.701 (OIG permissive exclusion, excessive charges); Fla. Stat. sec. 627.736(5)(a) (2026); 42 CFR 414.48; ECG Management Consultants, 'Capture Every Dollar: Chargemaster Maintenance Strategies for ASC Revenue Growth' (June 5, 2026)
practice_impact: Raise charges uniformly for all payers, read each Medicare Advantage and commercial agreement for charge-related clauses first, and expect no added Medicare revenue: gains arise only where a charge sat below a payer's allowed amount, and non-contracted Medicare Advantage claims stay capped at Original Medicare amounts (42 CFR 422.214).

claim: Contact each major payer's provider relations department and request the current contracted rate schedule. This data is available, payers are contractually required to provide it.
correct_statement: No universal contractual duty exists; access depends on each contract and on state law. Florida requires HMOs, by statute, to disclose the complete schedule of reimbursements to contracted physicians (confidentially); no parallel insurer mandate was found. Commercial plans' in-network rates are public under the federal Transparency in Coverage rule. Medicare Advantage contracts may fall outside both.
source_title: Fla. Stat. sec. 641.315(4)(d) (2026 Florida Statutes); 45 CFR 147.212(b) (Transparency in Coverage); 42 CFR 422.402 (Medicare Advantage preemption); American Medical News, July 31, 2009
practice_impact: Cite s. 641.315(4)(d) when asking HMOs for the full schedule; for other payers rely on the contract, the portal or public machine-readable files, and confirm each Medicare Advantage contract's stated percentage of Medicare.

claim: For most specialties, commercial contracted rates run between 120% and 180% of Medicare.
correct_statement: National averages fit the band: KFF's review found 143% of Medicare (studies ranged 118-179%); MedPAC reports 147% for 2024. But it is not a per-specialty rule: primary care and E/M run about 110-124%, three of 17 studied specialties exceed 180%, and states vary widely (Milliman 2024: 119-243%; HCCI 2017: Florida near 105-110%). The document cites no source.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy (March 2026), Ch. 4; KFF, 'How Much More Than Medicare Do Private Insurers Pay? A Review of the Literature' (2020); Urban Institute (Oct. 2021); HCCI (Aug. 2020); Milliman (June 2024)
practice_impact: Geriatrics is paid mostly by Medicare and Medicare Advantage (MA physician rates ran about 91-102% of traditional Medicare in a 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine study), so few contracts will approach 120-180%; verify actual rates before choosing a multiplier.

claim: Redetermination: the MA plan itself, 60 days to file, plan has 60 days to decide. Reconsideration: Independent Review Entity, 60 days to file after redetermination. ALJ hearing: $190+ claim threshold (2025). Federal Court: $1,900+ threshold (2025).
correct_statement: Part C level 1 is a plan 'reconsideration': file within 65 days of the denial notice; the plan decides in 30 days (pre-service) or 60 days (payment). Adverse decisions go to the IRE automatically. ALJ threshold is $200 for 2026 and 2027; federal court $1,960 for 2026, $2,000 for 2027. Contracted-provider payment disputes follow the contract instead.
source_title: CMS Managed Care Appeals pages (plan reconsideration, IRE, ALJ hearing, federal court; updated 11/03/2026); 42 CFR 422.582, 422.590, 422.600, 422.612; 91 FR 58681 (Sept. 16, 2026); CMS Parts C & D Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026)
practice_impact: A contracted practice cannot take an MA payment denial to the IRE or an ALJ; it must use the contract's dispute process, and enrollee-side appeals now have a 65-day window.

claim: Common codes like hypertension (I10) carry HCC weight; elevated blood pressure (R03.0) does not.
correct_statement: Essential hypertension (I10) maps to no CMS-HCC payment category in V22, V24 or V28, so it adds nothing to the Part C risk score; it maps only to RxHCC 187 in the Part D drug model. R03.0 maps to no model. Only hypertensive heart-failure or stage 5 CKD combination codes (such as I11.0, I12.0) map to V28 HCCs.
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings (2026 Model Software/ICD-10 Mappings); identical in 2027 Initial Mappings; 2025 Midyear/Final Mappings for the V24 column
practice_impact: Recapturing I10 on nursing-facility visits will not raise the Part C risk score (only a small Part D RxHCC weight); treating it as an HCC gap misdirects coding audits and shared-savings forecasts.

claim: Type 2 diabetes with diabetic chronic kidney disease (E11.65) has a much higher RAF impact than Type 2 diabetes uncomplicated (E11.9).
correct_statement: E11.65 is type 2 diabetes with hyperglycemia; diabetic CKD is E11.22. Under the V28 model used for all 2026 and 2027 payment, E11.9 and E11.65 both map to HCC 38, and HCCs 36, 37 and 38 share one coefficient (0.166 community non-dual aged, 0.280 institutional). Extra weight requires separately coding the CKD stage (N18.30 to N18.6).
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings and CMS-HCC V28 model software (relative factors); CY 2026 and CY 2027 Rate Announcements
practice_impact: Diabetes complication specificity alone no longer moves RAF; for long-stay residents the documentable gain is the CKD stage, heart-failure and other separately mapped conditions.

claim: MA plans ... may approve and pay a claim, then months later audit the medical record and recoup payment if the documentation does not support medical necessity - even if the authorization was obtained prospectively.
correct_statement: Since 2024, 42 CFR 422.138(c) bars an MA coordinated care plan that approved a service by prior authorization, pre-service or concurrent determination from later denying coverage for lack of medical necessity. It may reopen only for good cause or reliable evidence of fraud or similar fault; for approved inpatient admissions, later-gathered clinical information cannot supply good cause.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.138(c) Prior authorization and 42 CFR 422.616(e) (eCFR, current to 11/06/2026; 88 FR 22331, amended 90 FR 15910)
practice_impact: Matters only where the practice's services need plan authorization: a later medical-necessity clawback of an authorized service can be disputed under 422.138(c); documentation still matters for coding and fraud audits.

claim: MA plans deny claims on medical necessity grounds ... using proprietary clinical criteria that may differ from CMS national coverage determinations ... the InterQual criteria, the MCG guidelines, or the plan's own proprietary policy.
correct_statement: Plans do cite InterQual, MCG or their own policies, but since 2024 42 CFR 422.101(b)-(c) binds them to NCDs, LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules. Internal criteria are allowed only where Medicare criteria are not fully established, must rest on published evidence and be publicly posted, and may not otherwise be used to deny basic benefits.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6) and (c)(1) (eCFR, current to 11/06/2026); KFF, Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024 (Jan. 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Appeals should argue the service meets the NCD, LCD or Medicare rule and that proprietary criteria cannot override it, rather than only rebutting InterQual or MCG point by point.

claim: HCC diagnoses must be submitted at least once per calendar year for each patient to be included in that year's risk score calculation ... based on the ICD-10 diagnosis codes submitted on claims from all providers.
correct_statement: Annual recapture is real, but timing and scope are misstated. The model is prospective: diagnoses from 2026 dates of service set 2027 payment. Only diagnoses from face-to-face (or audio-video) encounters with physicians and other accepted practitioners, hospital inpatient or hospital outpatient providers count; for 2027 payment CMS also excludes audio-only visits and unlinked chart reviews.
source_title: CMS, Announcement of CY 2027 Medicare Advantage Capitation Rates and Part C and Part D Payment Policies (April 6, 2026); Medicare Managed Care Manual ch. 7; CY2026 Risk Adjustment Eligible CPT/HCPCS list
practice_impact: Your own nursing-facility visit claims (99304-99310 are risk-adjustment eligible) carry diagnoses into next year's payment; SNF facility claims, audio-only visits and plan chart reviews do not.

claim: Price transparency MRF data includes MA contracted rates alongside commercial rates.
correct_statement: Only hospital machine-readable files must list rates negotiated with Medicare Advantage plans. Payer Transparency in Coverage files, the ones holding physician-practice rates, cover non-grandfathered group and individual commercial coverage; the October 2026 final rule says MA is beyond its scope. A practice cannot benchmark its MA professional rates from payer files.
source_title: Transparency in Coverage final rule, 91 FR 63748 (Oct. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 147.212; CMS Hospital Price Transparency FAQs (current as of June 26, 2026)
practice_impact: Payer files will not show what MA plans pay other physician groups for facility visits; only hospital files (hospital-employed clinicians) carry MA rates, so benchmark against the Medicare fee schedule.

claim: HEDIS measures most relevant to physician practices include Transitions of Care (follow-up within 7/30 days post-discharge), Annual Wellness Visit (AWV completed in calendar year) and Medication Adherence (PDC > 80%).
correct_statement: Of the three, only Transitions of Care is a HEDIS measure, and its windows are 2 days for admission and discharge notices and 30 days for patient engagement and medication reconciliation, not 7/30. Medication adherence is a PQA Part D Star measure (PDC of 80% or higher). The Annual Wellness Visit is neither a HEDIS nor a Star Ratings measure.
source_title: CMS Medicare 2027 Part C & D Star Ratings Technical Notes (updated 11/04/2026); NCQA, Transitions of Care (TRC)
practice_impact: AWV bonuses are plan-contract incentives, not HEDIS; most HEDIS screening and diabetes measures exclude members 66+ in I-SNPs or long-term institutional care, so TRC and readmissions matter more.

claim: Milliman's 2025 Health Cost Guidelines research: commercial payers reimburse professional services at an average of 148 percent of Medicare fee-for-service rates; overall commercial rates average 196 percent; state-level range runs from 143 to 294 percent of Medicare.
A 2025 analysis by Aroris found that practices using structured data in their negotiations achieved average rate increases of 15.5 percent, compared to the industry average of 2 to 4 percent.

The No Surprises Act's price transparency requirements, effective since 2022, require payers to publish Machine-Readable Files (MRFs) containing their contracted rates with every provider in their network.
Prompt payment terms: Penalties for late payment (typically 1.5-2 percent per month after the required payment period).

If Humana is a significant commercial payer for your practice... Key strategic considerations for Humana commercial: Humana is generally willing to negotiate. Their provider relations team is accessible.

The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule is recalculated annually and has experienced a pattern of flat or declining conversion factor updates in recent years; any contract that pegs rates to Medicare participates in those declines automatically.

In most commercial contracts the renewal date is specified, typically with a 60 to 90 day termination notice requirement (Section 4); most commercial contracts require 90 to 180 days notice (Section 9).

Each major payer publishes a Table of Contents file listing MRF downloads: UnitedHealth Group transparency-in-coverage.uhc.com; Anthem anthem.com/machine-readable-file; Aetna aetna.com/transparency; Cigna cigna.com/legal/compliance/machine-readable-files; Humana humanatransparency.com.

National range for physician conversion factors is roughly $45 to $65 per wRVU; a primary care conversion factor of $48 is below the market median, $58 is on the high end, and a surgical $62 is competitive.

FMV (Fair Market Value): the value in arm's-length transactions consistent with general market value - the standard used by Stark Law to evaluate physician compensation; MGMA benchmarks are used as the primary FMV reference.

The MGMA Physician Compensation and Production Report, published annually, shows compensation at the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles; the MGMA benchmark figures represent total compensation - base salary plus all incentives and bonuses.

Some states - California is the most notable example - largely do not enforce physician non-competes on public policy grounds. Other states enforce them strictly. Many states evaluate non-competes on a reasonableness standard.
Courts in many states will interpret ambiguous non-compete terms against the employer who drafted them, but reaching that resolution requires litigation.

Tail coverage can cost one to three times your annual malpractice premium. For high-risk specialties that can be $30,000 to $100,000 or more. For a primary care physician, it might be $8,000 to $20,000.

Some agreements treat the signing bonus as taxable income at receipt but require repayment of the gross amount; you could pay taxes on $30,000, net $21,000, and then owe $30,000 back if you leave in month 18.

The practice collects typically 85% to 95% of allowed/collectible charges (the net collection rate) in a well-run practice; measured against billed charges (gross collection rate), the figure is commonly in the 50% to 80% range.
E/M up-coding (systematic): Repayment + 3x penalties under FCA; ~$14K-$28K per claim (2024-25 inflation-adjusted)
correct_statement: FCA liability is three times the government's damages plus a per-claim civil penalty, and only for 'knowing' false claims; it is not repayment plus 3x. The penalty is $14,308 to $28,619 per claim for penalties assessed after July 3, 2025; DOJ announced no increase for 2026, so that range still applies today.
source_title: 28 CFR 85.5, Table 1 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 90 FR 29447, July 3, 2025). Also: DOJ notice 'Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustments for 2026', 91 FR 43405, July 15, 2026 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/15/2026-14236/civil-monetary-penalties-inflation-adjustments-for-2026); 31 U.S.C. 3729(a)(1), (b)(1) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/3729)
practice_impact: Nursing-facility E/M levels (99304-99310) billed to Medicare/MA are the exposure: knowing or reckless upcoding risks treble damages plus up to $28,619 per claim, while honest errors still require refund within 60 days of identification (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7k(d)).

claim: Stark Law violations: $15K-$100K per violation; False Claims Act exposure
correct_statement: $15,000 and $100,000 are the unadjusted statutory amounts. Today the Stark civil monetary penalties are up to $31,670 per prohibited claim or service and up to $211,146 per circumvention arrangement or scheme, plus denial or refund of payment, assessments up to three times the amount claimed, possible exclusion, and False Claims Act exposure. HHS made no 2026 increase.
source_title: 45 CFR 102.3, Table 1 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 91 FR 3665, Jan. 28, 2026: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/28/2026-01688/annual-civil-monetary-penalties-inflation-adjustment). Also: HHS notice 'No Adjustment to HHS Civil Monetary Penalty Amounts for 2026', 91 FR 66566 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/21/2026-21524/no-adjustment-to-hhs-civil-monetary-penalty-amounts-for-2026); 42 U.S.C. 1395nn(g)(3)-(4); 42 CFR 1003.310; Fla. Stat. 456.053(5)(e)-(f)
practice_impact: Financial relationships with labs, therapy, DME, home-health or facility entities the physicians refer to (including medical-director pay) are the Stark-sensitive areas; per-claim exposure is about double the vendor's figure, and Florida's Patient Self-Referral Act (s. 456.053) adds $15,000/$100,000 state penalties across all payers.

claim: HIPAA breach - unsecured PHI: $100-$50,000 per violation; up to $1.9M per category/year
correct_statement: Current HIPAA penalties per violation run from $145-$73,011 (no knowledge) to $73,011-$2,190,294 (uncorrected willful neglect), with a $2,190,294 calendar-year cap per identical provision; OCR applies lower annual caps to lower tiers under its 2019 enforcement discretion. $100-$50,000 is the unadjusted statute and $1.9M was the 2022 cap. HHS made no 2026 increase.
source_title: 45 CFR 102.3, Table 1, rows for 42 U.S.C. 1320d-5 / 45 CFR 160.404 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 91 FR 3665, Jan. 28, 2026). Also: HHS notice 91 FR 66566, Oct. 21, 2026 (no 2026 adjustment); Notification of Enforcement Discretion Regarding HIPAA Civil Money Penalties, 84 FR 18151, Apr. 30, 2019 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/04/30/2019-08530/notification-of-enforcement-discretion-regarding-hipaa-civil-money-penalties); Fla. Stat. 501.171
practice_impact: Unencrypted laptops or phones used on facility rounds are the obvious unsecured-PHI risk; per-violation ceilings are about 46% above the vendor's figure, and Florida's FIPA (s. 501.171) separately requires notice within 30 days with penalties up to $500,000.

claim: Timely filing failure: 100% denial; no appeal pathway. Prevention: Submission within 72 hours of encounter
correct_statement: Late claims are denied, but deadlines and remedies differ by payer. Medicare: one calendar year from date of service; the denial is not appealable, though 42 CFR 424.44(b) grants four exceptions. Florida insurers and HMOs: six months (secondary 90 days), with statutory dispute resolution. Medicaid: 12 months. Submission within 72 hours is a vendor target, not a rule.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 1, ss. 70, 70.4, 70.6, 70.7 (Rev. 12909, issued 10-24-24). Also: 42 CFR 424.44; First Coast Service Options, 'What is the claim timely filing guideline?' (https://medicare.fcso.com/node/5026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b), (8) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/627.6131); Fla. Stat. 408.7057; 42 CFR 447.45(d)(1)
practice_impact: First Coast denies Part B claims received more than 12 months after the date of service (CO-29), and claims rejected as unprocessable do not count as filed; Florida commercial/HMO claims have only six months and secondary claims 90 days after the primary's determination.

claim: Typical reimbursement vs. Medicare: Medicare Advantage 85-110% of Medicare; Medicaid 50-80% of Medicare (state-dependent)
correct_statement: MA physician prices cluster near 100% of Medicare: studies of 2007-2014 claims found 91%-102% across common physician services (97% for 99213), and non-contracted providers receive the Original Medicare amount. Medicaid fees averaged 75% of Medicare nationally in 2024, ranging 52%-132% by state, with 27 of 50 programs above 80%. Florida: 64% overall, 56% primary care.
source_title: KFF State Health Facts, Medicaid-to-Medicare Fee Index (2024 and 2019), sourced to Skopec, Pugazhendhi, Zuckerman, Health Affairs 2025;44(5):531-538 (https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.01530). According to PubMed: Trish et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017;177(9):1287-1295 (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.2679); Pelech, Med Care Res Rev 2020;77(3):236-248 (https://doi.org/10.1177/1077558718780604). Also: 42 CFR 422.214; Fla. Stat. 409.908(13)(b) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/409.908); CMS QMB billing protections (https://www.cms.gov/medicare/medicaid-coordination/qualified-medicare-beneficiary-program)
practice_impact: For dual-eligible residents Florida Medicaid pays nothing toward Medicare coinsurance when Medicare's payment already meets the Medicaid rate (s. 409.908(13)(b)) and QMBs cannot be billed, so those visits collect only Medicare's 80% share; check each MA contract's actual percent of Medicare.

claim: For independent physician practices, multiples typically range from 2x to 6x [EBITDA]; Primary care: 3-5x. Revenue multiples for physician practices typically range from 0.5x to 1.5x net revenue
correct_statement: No authoritative dataset was found supporting these ranges. MedPAC (2021, citing Casalino 2019) reports 8-12x EBITDA for large platform practices and 2-4x or less for small add-on practices, with EBITDA typically created by cutting owner-physician pay about 30%. The primary care 3-5x and 0.5-1.5x revenue figures have no traceable source; treat them as broker rules of thumb.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare and the Health Care Delivery System, June 2021, Chapter 3 'Congressional request: Private equity and Medicare' (text and endnote 32, citing Casalino et al. 2019 and Helm 2019). Context only, no numeric ranges: Physicians Practice, 'Medical practice valuations', May 29, 2024 (https://www.physicianspractice.com/view/medical-practice-valuations)
practice_impact: A small physician-owned geriatrics practice that pays out its profit as physician compensation has little normalized EBITDA, so a multiple may produce a low value; a sale to a hospital or other referral recipient must be at appraised fair market value under Stark/AKS.

claim: Family Medicine median updated to ~5,200 wRVUs/year per recent MGMA-derived benchmark data; 75th percentile 6,100. Internal Medicine median 4,000; 75th percentile 4,900
correct_statement: MGMA specialty percentile tables are paywalled, so 5,200 and 6,100 cannot be confirmed exactly; MGMA's public charts show 2024 primary care median wRVUs of about 5,200 (physician-owned) and 5,550 (hospital-owned). A 4,000 internal medicine median is well below published benchmarks: AMGA's 2026 survey reports medians of 6,505 for family medicine and 6,390 for internal medicine.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026; 2025 data). Also: MGMA, 'Key Insights: 2025 Provider Compensation and Productivity Trends and Benchmarks' with median work RVU charts (2024 data) (https://www.mgma.com/2025-provider-compensation); MGMA 2024 Provider Compensation Data Report (2023 data) (https://www.mgma.com/getkaiasset/252744ee-c63b-4a96-9211-8a5d6b908b39/MGMA-2024-Provider-Compensation-Data-Report.pdf)
practice_impact: Office-based family/internal medicine medians are the wrong yardstick for nursing-facility geriatrics, and a 4,000 'median' would understate targets by roughly a quarter to a third; license the MGMA or AMGA geriatrics line before benchmarking productivity or setting compensation.

claim: Set your fee schedule at a minimum of 200-250% of Medicare. Anything lower is a structural leak.
correct_statement: No CMS, AMA or MGMA standard was found setting a 200-250% floor; it is a rule of thumb. Payers pay the lesser of charge or allowable, so charges need only exceed the highest allowable per code. In Florida the top statutory allowables are PIP at 200% of Medicare and workers' compensation at 175% (210% surgical), so about 200-210% is defensible.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.736(5)(a) (2026 Florida Statutes). Also: Fla. Stat. 440.13(12)(f)-(g) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/440.13); 42 U.S.C. 1395w-4(a)(1) (Medicare pays the lesser of actual charge or fee schedule amount) and 1395w-4(g) limiting charge (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1395w-4); 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(b)(6)(A); AAPC member forum threads stating there is no rule or regulation for setting fees (https://www.aapc.com/discuss/threads/determining-how-much-to-set-your-fee-schedule.193884/)
practice_impact: Medicare, MA and Medicaid pay fixed allowables, so higher charges add nothing from them; the level matters only for auto/PIP, workers' comp, out-of-network and self-pay accounts, and one uniform schedule is needed because charging Medicare substantially more than usual charges risks exclusion (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(b)(6)).

claim: Stark exceptions require that compensation arrangements be set in advance, in writing, for a period of at least one year. They must be signed by all parties. Oral arrangements do not qualify.
correct_statement: Only some Stark exceptions require this. Personal service arrangements and office or equipment leases must be written, signed and last at least one year. Bona fide employment (42 CFR 411.357(c)) and group-practice pay need no writing, signature or term; the fair-market-value exception has no minimum term; limited remuneration (up to $6,237 in 2026) needs no writing.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(c), (d), (l), (z) and 411.354(e) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026; last amended 2023); CMS Phase II interim final rule, 69 FR 16054, 16067-68 (Mar. 26, 2004); CMS Physician Self-Referral CPI-U Updates page (CY 2026 limited remuneration limit $6,237)
practice_impact: Employed physicians need no one-year written Stark contract (written agreements remain prudent); the writing, signature and one-year rules bite on independent-contractor and medical-director agreements with SNFs, hospices, home health agencies, hospitals and labs.

claim: Arrangements that have lapsed, where the written agreement has expired but the arrangement continues, lose their Stark exception protection until a new agreement is executed.
correct_statement: Since Jan. 1, 2016, an expired lease or personal service agreement of at least one year stays protected indefinitely as a holdover if it continues on the same terms and still meets every exception requirement, including fair market value. Protection is lost only if terms change or a requirement fails. Employment arrangements never needed a writing.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(a)(7), (b)(6), (d)(1)(vii), (l)(2) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); CY 2016 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 80 FR 70886, 71318-71320 (Nov. 16, 2015), effective Jan. 1, 2016 (govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2015-11-16/html/2015-28005.htm)
practice_impact: Medical-director or contractor agreements with SNFs, hospices or home health agencies that expired but continued unchanged are likely still protected if records show identical terms; do not refund or self-disclose on the vendor's reading without counsel, and re-paper before changing pay or duties.

claim: Compensation under a Stark exception cannot be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals. This prohibition is absolute. A productivity bonus based partly on referral volume, even indirectly, violates Stark.
correct_statement: Most compensation exceptions bar pay that takes referral volume or value into account, but not absolutely. Since 2021 the test is met only if referrals are a variable in the formula. Group practices may pay profit shares indirectly reflecting designated health services and bonuses on personally performed and incident-to services; value-based and physician-incentive-plan exceptions carry no such bar.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.354(d)(5), 411.352(g) and (i), 411.357(c)(4), (d)(2), (aa) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, final rule, 85 FR 77492, 77537-38 and 77559 (Dec. 2, 2020)
practice_impact: wRVU bonuses on personally performed facility visits are expressly permitted; never put home health, lab, therapy, DME or hospital referrals into a pay formula. Florida's all-payer kickback and patient-brokering laws (ss. 456.054, 817.505) also reach referral-based pay.

claim: A physician-owner earning $600,000 per year in a market where the FMV for their specialty and productivity is $350,000 has a $250,000 annual exposure that does not disappear because the physician holds an ownership stake.
correct_statement: Stark imposes no fair-market-value test on what a physician-owned group practice pays its owners. Their in-practice referrals rest on the in-office ancillary services exception and group-practice rules, which bar only pay tied directly to referral volume or value. Stark liability is refund of tainted designated-health-service claims plus penalties up to $31,670 per service, not the pay gap.
source_title: CMS Phase II interim final rule, 69 FR 16054, 16067-68 (Mar. 26, 2004); 42 CFR 411.351, 411.352, 411.353, 411.355(a)-(b) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 102.3 (as amended at 91 FR 3666, Jan. 28, 2026); IRS, S corporation compensation and medical insurance issues (reviewed Mar. 3, 2026)
practice_impact: A practice billing only visits and care management (no lab, imaging, therapy, DME) furnishes no designated health services, so Stark does not police owner pay, and Florida s. 817.505(3)(b) likewise exempts payments within a group practice; owner pay is a tax, anti-kickback and buyer-diligence question.

claim: The FMV standard is met when compensation falls within the range supported by objective, commercially reasonable evidence, typically benchmark survey data from recognized sources such as MGMA or AMGA.
correct_statement: Stark defines fair market value as the value in an arm's-length transaction consistent with general market value: what well-informed parties not positioned to generate business for each other would pay. CMS calls salary surveys an appropriate starting point, sometimes sufficient, but rejects any percentile safe harbor. Commercial reasonableness is a separate requirement, not the evidentiary standard for FMV.
source_title: Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, final rule, 85 FR 77492, 77555-58 (Dec. 2, 2020); 42 CFR 411.351 definitions of fair market value, general market value and commercially reasonable (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Matching an MGMA or AMGA percentile is not a safe harbor; medical-director stipends and facility-based geriatric pay need documented duties, hours and local market facts, using geriatrics-specific survey cuts rather than generic primary care medians.

claim: Nationally, conversion factors generally range from approximately $45 to $65 per wRVU... A primary care physician may have a conversion factor in the $45 to $55 range. A proceduralist may command $55 to $65 or higher.
correct_statement: The $45-$65 national band has no cited source. AMGA's 2026 survey (2025 data) reports median compensation-per-wRVU ratios of $50.52-$55.62 in primary care (family medicine $52.61), consistent with the claim, but $68.79 cardiology, $72.28 gastroenterology, $74.48 general surgery and $78.94 orthopedics, above the stated range. These are all-in pay ratios, not contract rates.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026; 2025 data from 451 groups, about 188,000 providers). Practice-impact figures computed from CMS RVU26D relative value and GPCI files (released Aug. 26, 2026) and Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12, sec. 20.4.2
practice_impact: Medicare's 2026 Florida allowed amount is only about $51-$56 per wRVU for SNF visits 99308-99310 (POS 31) and $59-$65 in POS 32, before sequestration and overhead; a $45-$55 conversion factor could consume nearly all visit revenue.

claim: Typical primary care (illustrative): 25th percentile ~3,500 wRVUs/year and ~$157,500; median ~4,500 and ~$220,500; 75th ~5,500 and ~$286,000; 90th ~6,500 and ~$357,500 total comp.
correct_statement: The table is not survey data: each pay figure is wRVUs times an assumed $45-$55, and it sits far below current benchmarks. AMGA's 2026 survey (2025 data) reports medians of 6,505 wRVUs and $342,411 for family medicine and 6,390 and $361,426 for internal medicine. MedPAC reports $308,000 median primary care compensation for 2024. Percentile tables are paywalled.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026); MedPAC, March 2026 Report to the Congress, ch. 4, pp. 128-129 (SullivanCotter 2025 survey, 2024 pay; medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch4_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf); MGMA, Key Insights: 2025 Provider Compensation and Productivity Trends and Benchmarks (mgma.com/2025-provider-compensation)
practice_impact: Benchmarking against this table would understate market pay by roughly a third and label a median producer as 90th percentile; buy geriatrics-specific MGMA or AMGA cuts, since public medians reflect general primary care, not nursing-facility practice.

claim: wRVUs do not reflect administrative work, care coordination, supervision of mid-levels, teaching, committee participation, or any non-clinical contribution a physician makes to the practice.
correct_statement: Unbilled administrative, committee and teaching time earns no wRVUs, but care coordination does when billed: in 2026 Medicare assigns 1.00 wRVU to chronic care management (99490), 2.78-3.79 to transitional care management, 1.50 to advance care planning and 1.73 to care plan oversight. Incident-to and split/shared services by nurse practitioners can also bill under the physician.
source_title: CMS, 2026 National Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File, October release (RVU26D, released Aug. 26, 2026); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions About Practitioner Billing for Chronic Care Management Services (updated Aug. 16, 2022); 42 CFR 410.26 and 415.140 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Care management, transitional care, advance care planning and cognitive assessment are core geriatrics revenue, and CMS says CCM is billable for SNF, nursing facility and assisted living patients; the comp plan must state who gets that wRVU credit.

claim: The contract may limit how you export [your patient data], charge fees for data extraction, or restrict the format in which data is returned if you leave.
Patient responsibility now represents 25 to 35 percent of independent practice revenue.
Vendor liability is typically capped at the amount paid in the prior month or quarter.
A clearinghouse with a 3% lower first-pass acceptance rate, at 500 claims per month, produces 180 additional denied claims annually, each needing follow-up and often only partial recovery.

Minimum standard: a live real-time eligibility check should return copay, deductible, and auth requirements, not just active coverage, with alerts for authorization requirements and benefit limitations.
Data migration ranges from $5,000 to $50,000+ depending on data volume and complexity.

A portal that converts 85% of statement recipients into payers versus one that converts 60% is a gap entirely attributable to friction in the payment process; 90-day target: payment completion rate above 70%.
A system transition typically brings 30 to 90 days of reduced efficiency, and 60 to 90 days before staff reach pre-transition efficiency; buffer with a cash reserve equal to 2 months of expenses.
Claims submitted during a Medicare deactivation period are not retroactively compensable after billing privileges are reactivated; the gap is a permanent revenue loss, not a delay.

Medicare sets the effective date as the later of the application filing date or the date services first began at the enrolled location; retroactive billing is permitted up to 30 days prior when circumstances precluded advance enrollment.

Start commercial payer credentialing a minimum of 120 days before a new provider is scheduled to see patients. Start Medicare enrollment 90 days out. [Onboarding table: submit Medicare PECOS enrollment 120 days before start.]

Most providers revalidate Medicare enrollment every five years (DMEPOS suppliers every three); due dates are published on the Medicare Revalidation List at data.cms.gov and are updated seven months before the deadline.
CMS launched PECOS 2.0 in late 2025, replacing the legacy enrollment portal; legacy PECOS credentials and workflows do not transfer automatically and the transition requires account re-configuration.
CAQH ProView requires re-attestation every 120 days; a profile not attested within 120 days moves to Expired status. Illinois operates on a 180-day window, the only state with a different standard.
Medicare allows billing under the supervising physician's NPI for locum arrangements that meet the Q6 modifier requirements.
Medicaid does not grant retroactive effective dates in most circumstances; unlike Medicare, there is generally no retroactive billing right for services before the enrollment effective date.
File as early as legally possible, which is 30 days before the practice opens.

Medicare enrollment for a new practice requires two applications, the CMS-855I ... and the CMS-855B ... Submit CMS-855B first, the organizational enrollment must be in process before the individual reassignment (CMS-855R) ... can be submitted

The Medicare effective date cannot precede the date of the application ... Do not see Medicare patients until enrollment is confirmed, billing Medicare for services rendered before the effective enrollment date is a compliance violation
Non-enrolled payers cannot be billed at all ... Revenue generated in months 1, 3 from unenrolled payers cannot be recovered retroactively in most cases.
Medicare enrollment applications require active management and response to information requests within 30 days or the application is rejected
Set a calendar reminder to re-attest every 120 days, CAQH profiles expire and an expired profile will pause enrollment applications mid-process
Financial hardship policy, define the income threshold (typically based on federal poverty guidelines) ... The policy must be applied consistently to avoid HIPAA and anti-discrimination exposure.
set list-price fees in the range of 200 to 250 percent of Medicare allowables ... you can never collect more than your billed charge, even if the contracted rate is higher
In most independent practices, a substantial and growing share of total revenue - commonly cited in the range of 25 to 35 percent - comes directly from patients.
By the time an account reaches a third-party collector, practices typically recover roughly 20 to 30 cents on the dollar, and pay a percentage of that to the collection agency.
Copay is collected before the patient is roomed, every visit, no exceptions. Outstanding balances are addressed at check-in, not deferred to statements.
It does not have to be exact - estimates are standard and expected; confirm your state's estimate-disclosure and good-faith-estimate requirements with counsel.

Automatic payment required: the patient provides a credit card, debit card, or bank account for automatic monthly drafts. Written terms: the patient signs (or digitally acknowledges) the payment plan terms, including the monthly amount and payment dates.
Proactive hardship identification converts what would become a write-off into either a reduced-fee arrangement (which is collectible) or a formal charity designation.
A formal charity designation is appropriately written off and potentially tax-advantaged.

A practice with a well-functioning point-of-service collection system and effective statement cycle should collect 90 cents or more of every patient-responsibility dollar. Practices without front-end collection processes typically land in the 60-75% range.

Medicare participation does not transfer in an asset acquisition, the acquiring entity must enroll in Medicare under its own NPI and PTAN, and the acquired providers must be enrolled under the new entity's NPI and group in PECOS.
This process takes 30 to 60 days from completed application submission. During the Medicare enrollment gap, claims submitted to Medicare under the new entity will be rejected.
The right path: begin PECOS enrollment 90+ days before close; target enrollment approval at or before close.
NEVER attempt to bill Medicare under the acquired practice's legacy credentials after the ownership change has occurred, this creates False Claims Act exposure for the acquirer.
Compliance issues from the pre-close period can become the acquirer's problem in an asset acquisition if not identified and addressed in the deal structure.

A standard AR quality adjustment applies collection probability by age bucket: 0, 30 days 95, 98 percent, 31, 60 days 85, 90 percent, 61, 90 days 70, 80 percent, 91, 120 days 50, 65 percent, 120-plus days 20, 40 percent.
Average revenue disruption in an unmanaged practice acquisition transition: 15, 25% of monthly collections for 60, 90 days post-close ... can be reduced to less than 5% and resolved within 30 days.

Most PE-backed physician practice acquisitions use a Management Services Organization (MSO) structure ... The physician entity remains the billing entity ... payer contracts are in the physician entity's name, and revenue belongs to the physician entity.

Medicare withdrawal must be completed within 90 days of the decision to retire or close, through PECOS; DMEPOS suppliers have 30 days. The clock starts when the decision is made, not when the last patient is seen.

Medicare Fee-for-Service providers must retain all documentation supporting Medicare claims for a minimum of six years from creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later; the requirement is grounded in HIPAA's administrative simplification rules (45 CFR 164.316).

Medicare managed care and Medicare Advantage providers face a longer retention requirement: patient records must be kept for a minimum of ten years, regardless of the shorter six-year federal FFS standard.
State medical record retention example for Florida: 5 years from the date of last patient contact.

A practice with primarily commercial payers that pay in 30 to 45 days can stop new patients closer to closing; high Medicare and Medicaid volume, where payment cycles can run 60 to 90 days, needs more lead time.

If the final audit finds overpayment risk, the physician has three choices: remediate before submitting final claims, self-disclose identified overpayments to CMS (via the CMS Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol or OIG's self-disclosure protocol), or accept the post-closure audit risk.

Medicare and Medicaid receivables cannot be directly assigned to third parties; factoring companies use sweep account structures where the account remains in the practice's name and the factoring company receives funds as payers remit.
The final audit should test whether documented E&M visit levels are supported by the clinical documentation, 'using the current 2021 AMA/CMS E&M guidelines.'
E&M code distribution, the count and percentage of visits billed at each level (99211, 99215 for established patients, 99201, 99205 for new patients)
The False Claims Act creates civil liability for submitting false or fraudulent claims to government healthcare programs ... with treble damages and program exclusion as potential penalties.
Voluntary self-disclosure to CMS or other agencies may be appropriate for significant Medicare overpayments, a legal decision requiring healthcare M&A counsel
in an asset sale, the seller typically retains the pre-close AR; in a stock sale, the AR stays with the entity.
Stark Law and Anti-Kickback: are all physician compensation arrangements, space and equipment leases, and referral relationships structured within applicable safe harbors?

private equity completing 79 physician practice deals in Q1 2025 alone ... (FOCUS Investment Banking; Sofer Advisors) ... the median healthcare services EV/EBITDA multiple compressed to roughly 11.5x in 2025 from 14.5x in 2024
Primary care, small/solo: typical EBITDA multiple 3, 5x; primary care, scaled/platform: 6, 10x+, with value-based care outperformers reaching double-digit multiples.
Industry standards suggest that AR over 120 days is collectible at roughly 50 cents on the dollar; over 180 days, 20 to 30 cents; over 360 days, essentially a write-off.
During the credentialing period, claims can often be submitted under a supervising provider's NPI, but this requires explicit verification with each payer [and documented supervision].
Until a provider is fully credentialed with every relevant payer, their claims cannot be submitted under their NPI.
Medicare: 60, 90 days from complete application submission ... The credentialing process must begin at least 90 days before a new provider sees their first patient.
Never ignore an audit letter. Non-response is treated as an admission and triggers automatic recoupment.
An RCM vendor without a current BAA is not HIPAA-compliant, and using them exposes the practice to HIPAA liability. It should be a standalone agreement, not embedded in the service contract.
The vendor's fee typically ranges from 4, 9% of net collections ... with the current market average tracking between 5.5% and 7.2% for full-service billing across practice types.
AR that ages past 120 days has collection probability below 40% for commercial payers and below 20% for some government payers.
Medicaid: 60, 120 days, with significant state variation; Commercial payers: 30, 90 days, depending on payer and network status; Hospital-based credentialing: 90, 180 days.

Average fully-loaded cost of replacing a billing staff member (recruiting, training, productivity gap) is 50 to 100 percent of annual salary; a biller earning $50,000 costs $25,000 to $50,000 to replace.
Medical Biller national median base pay as of 2025: $36,000, $44,000 entry (0, 2 yrs), $42,000, $52,000 mid (3, 5 yrs), $50,000, $62,000 experienced (6+ yrs).
Medical Coder, CPC national median base pay as of 2025: $42,000, $52,000 entry, $50,000, $62,000 mid, $58,000, $74,000 experienced; certification adds +5, 12% at the same experience level.
Medical Coder, CPC-H (hospital): key compensation factors are hospital coding complexity, DRG and APC experience; pay a +5, 12% premium for CPC, CPC-H, or CPMA certification.

Revenue Cycle Manager base pay: $62,000, $78,000 in a 1, 5 provider practice, $72,000, $90,000 at 6, 15 providers, $84,000, $105,000 at 16+ providers; Revenue Cycle Director $88,000, $110,000 in a small practice.
For staff at market rate and meeting performance targets: cost-of-living adjustment (typically CPI-based, 3, 5%); for staff exceeding performance targets: merit increase above CPI, up to 8%.

Geographic adjustment to national median: Tier 2 high-cost markets (Chicago, Miami, Denver, San Diego, Portland, Austin, Minneapolis) +10, 20%; Tier 4 lower-cost markets (most mid-size and smaller metros, rural), 5, 15%; fully remote roles +5, 10%.

Medical Coder strong performance: coding accuracy >=95% on audit and E&M within 10% of specialty norm; intervention needed if accuracy is below 90% or E&M distribution is significantly outside norms in either direction.

CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule permanently removed telehealth frequency limits for subsequent inpatient visits, subsequent nursing facility visits, and critical care consultation services; no maximum number of telehealth encounters per episode or time period.
correct_statement: H.R. 7148 became P.L. 119-75 on February 3, 2026. Section 6209 extends Medicare telehealth flexibilities (home and any geography, practitioner list, audio-only, FQHC/RHC) through December 31, 2027. The tele-mental-health in-person requirement applies to services on or after January 1, 2028, so the waiver ends December 31, 2027, one day earlier than the vendor's wording.
source_title: H.R. 7148, Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), enrolled text, sec. 6209; CMS Telehealth FAQ updated 10/8/2026; telehealth.hhs.gov telehealth policy updates
practice_impact: Telehealth to home, assisted-living and facility patients stays billable without rural limits through 2027; from January 1, 2028, absent new law, non-behavioral telehealth again needs a rural facility site, which most Florida metro facilities are not.

claim: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, signed February 3, 2026, extends most Medicare telehealth flexibilities through December 31, 2027; the next potential cliff date is January 1, 2028 unless Congress acts again.
correct_statement: Correct. The CY 2026 PFS final rule (CMS-1832-F), effective January 1, 2026, permanently removed Medicare telehealth frequency limits for subsequent inpatient visits (99231-99233), subsequent nursing facility visits (99307-99310) and critical care consultations (G0508, G0509). Earlier caps were one visit every 3 days, one every 14 days and one per day.
source_title: CMS fact sheet, Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F)
practice_impact: High: removes the one-per-14-days cap on telehealth follow-ups for nursing facility residents; federally mandated periodic visits still must be in person under CMS manual guidance (verify current text), and POS 02 pays the facility rate.

claim: Effective January 1, 2026, CMS made permanent direct supervision of incident-to services via real-time, two-way audio-video technology under the CY 2026 PFS final rule; the supervising physician need not be physically present in the office suite.
correct_statement: Correct with a carve-out. Since January 1, 2026 (CY 2026 PFS final rule, not the 2026 appropriations act), 42 CFR 410.26(a)(2) allows direct supervision by real-time audio/video presence, not audio-only, except for services with a 010 or 090 global surgery indicator. The supervisor must remain immediately available.
source_title: eCFR, 42 CFR 410.26 (incident-to conditions; direct supervision definition); CMS fact sheet, CY 2026 PFS final rule (CMS-1832-F)
practice_impact: Limited: incident-to billing is barred in hospitals and SNFs (42 CFR 410.26(b)(1)), so this helps only office, home or assisted-living services; per the CY 2027 final rule, incident-to telehealth claims need new modifier BC from January 1, 2027.

claim: POS 10 (patient at home) is paid at the non-facility rate and POS 02 (patient not at home) at the facility rate; the difference for the same service runs roughly 10 to 25 percent depending on code and locality.
correct_statement: Correct in context. CPT deleted 99441-99443 for 2025; Medicare audio-only E/M uses 99202-99215 with modifier 93, only for patients at home. CMS gave 98000-98015 status indicator I (not valid for Medicare). The playbook omits that 98016, the brief virtual check-in that replaced G2012, is payable by Medicare.
source_title: CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2024-25382, published December 9, 2024); telehealth.hhs.gov Medicare FFS billing page
practice_impact: Moderate: retire 99441-99443 and keep 98000-98015 off Medicare claims, but keep 98016 for virtual check-ins; audio-only E/M applies only to patients at home, not nursing facility residents.

claim: Codes 99441, 99442 and 99443 were eliminated from the CPT code set effective January 1, 2025; Medicare audio-only E&M uses 99202-99215 with modifier 93; the 98000-series codes are NOT accepted by Medicare.
correct_statement: POS 10 pays the non-facility rate and POS 02 the facility rate. In 2026 the gap for office visits is about 35-40% (99213: 2.85 vs 1.72 total RVUs; 99214: $135.61 vs $84.50) after CMS halved facility indirect practice expense; nursing facility codes differ about 12-14%.
source_title: CMS Transmittal 12671, CR 13582 (Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 sec. 10.5); 2026 PFS amounts via third-party fee-schedule lookups; AMA 2026 final rule summary
practice_impact: High: telehealth to a nursing facility resident is POS 02 (facility rate, about 12-14% below POS 32 in 2026, equalized for 2027); a wrong POS on home visits costs roughly 35-40%, not 10-25%. Confirm on the First Coast fee schedule.

claim: The clinical record for every audio-only claim must document audio-only delivery and the reason (patient lacked video capability or declined video); service must be to a patient at home; missing rationale leaves a paid claim vulnerable to recoupment.
correct_statement: Audio-only for non-behavioral services runs through December 31, 2027, for patients at home when the practitioner is video-capable and the patient cannot or will not use video. CMS requires modifier 93 as the attestation and stated no additional documentation is needed; a note explaining why is prudent, not a CMS requirement.
source_title: CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2024-25382); 42 CFR 410.78(a)(3); telehealth.hhs.gov telehealth policy updates; First Coast telehealth services page
practice_impact: High: nursing facility residents are not 'at home', so audio-only visits to them are not billable telehealth; use audio-only only for patients in a private residence and keep a brief reason in the note for audit defense.

claim: CCM (99490/99491/99487/99489) and RPM (99453/99454/99457/99458) are not telehealth services in the Medicare definition; they cannot be billed using telehealth POS codes or modifiers, and doing so is incorrect coding.
correct_statement: CCM and RPM are non-face-to-face services outside the Medicare telehealth rules; no POS 02/10 or telehealth modifiers. The code lists are incomplete: CCM also uses add-ons 99439 and 99437; RPM also includes 99091 and, since January 1, 2026, 99445 (2-15 days of data) and 99470 (10-19 minutes).
source_title: CMS Telehealth FAQ (updated 10/8/2026); CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2025-19787); CMS MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services
practice_impact: Moderate: relevant mainly to home and assisted-living panels; a charge master built from the vendor's list would miss CCM add-ons and the 2026 RPM codes.

claim: Telehealth payment parity for fully insured commercial plans is governed by state law; more than 40 states (44 states plus D.C. as of 2026) have some form of telehealth parity law.
correct_statement: No traceable source shows that most Medicare Advantage plans require modifier 95; rules vary by plan. UnitedHealthcare MA and Humana key telehealth to POS 02/10; Florida Blue MA wants modifier 93 or 95 plus POS 02/10. CMS's claims manual itself pairs POS 02/10 with modifier 93 or 95 for Original Medicare.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage Telehealth and Telemedicine Policy, Professional; Humana Medicare telehealth FAQ; Florida Blue payment policy 20-069 Virtual Visits; Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 sec. 10.5
practice_impact: Verify each Florida MA plan's telehealth rule in writing (Humana, UnitedHealthcare, Florida Blue and others); a blanket 95 assumption risks denials, and Medicare adds modifiers BB and BC on January 1, 2027.

claim: Small practices - fewer than 16 clinicians in the practice's MIPS-eligible group - receive automatic reweighting ... Promoting Interoperability drops to 0%, ... Quality rises to 40% and Improvement Activities to 30%, keeping Cost at 30%.

CMS has finalized 75 points as the MIPS performance threshold and will maintain it through the 2028 performance year ... Below 75, the payment adjustment scales down linearly, reaching the full -9% cap at scores of 18.75 points or lower.
there is no lump-sum APM bonus for the 2025 performance year or later under current law ... For CY2026, this produced a final conversion factor of $33.5675 for QPs ... versus $33.4009 for non-QPs
MVP registration must be completed before the performance year begins - a practice cannot retroactively elect an MVP pathway partway through the year.
Improvement Activities 15% - Attestation-based; at least one high-weighted or two medium-weighted activities the practice is actually performing.

Maximum positive adjustment actually paid: +1.05% for the 2026 payment year (the lowest in the program's history); 2025 payment year +2.15%; 2023 payment year +2.34%; and an anomalous spike to +8.25% for the 2024 payment year.

A practice still coding to V24-era habits - documenting 'chronic kidney disease' without a stage, or 'diabetes' without a documented complication - is systematically under-capturing RAF for its MA panel
